title: Normative requirements derived from Gujarat's own instruments
note: Holds only what Gujarat's own instruments require of a system running a cheque case, or where a Gujarat instrument tightens a national obligation. Nothing here restates central law. The SARAS Courts Rules, 2026 are the deepest source, because they are written for cheque cases alone: the electronic record on the designated portal is the primary and authoritative judicial record, the original cheque is retained through trial and returned only on an endorsement, chief examination is tendered by e-filed affidavit while cross-examination stays physical, and the whole regime sits on the 2024 e-Filing SOP and the 2025 video conferencing rules. Where a requirement tightens a national one, tightens is left null and tightens_hint describes the national obligation for resolution once the national file is merged. Two caveats on sources: the Criminal Manual, 1977 AKN is OCR'd from a scan of the first edition and is rough in places, so requirements drawn from it stay with passages that read cleanly, and its process-fee and search-fee figures are the 1977 table and are flagged as such; and the SARAS press release is a record of two notifications that are not themselves in the corpus, so requirements resting on it are marked derivedFrom practice-note.

requirements.statement: The system MUST institute a cheque case e-filed by a bank or an NBFC in the SARAS N.I. Court establishment under the case type 'eCriminal Case'.
requirements.why: The SARAS establishment is a sub-establishment of the C.J.M. courts of Ahmedabad City and its docket is identified by that exact case-type string. A system that files the same complaint as an ordinary 'Criminal Case' puts it on the conventional C.J.M. board, where it is neither allocated to a nominated remote-adjudication presiding officer nor picked up by the SARAS cause list, and the filer discovers the misrouting only when the matter fails to appear.

binds.target: case record - case type of a SARAS N.I. cheque case

requirements.how: The case type is recorded as the literal string 'eCriminal Case'.
requirements.test: Case instituted through the SARAS route carries case type 'eCriminal Case'; a case with any other case type is not allocated to a SARAS presiding officer.
requirements.statusReason: Paragraph 3 records that the SARAS N.I. Court establishment was set up under the C.J.M. Courts of Ahmedabad City exclusively for cheque cases e-filed by banks and NBFCs, and says in terms that these cases will be filed and instituted with case type 'eCriminal Case'; rule 1(c) applies the SARAS rules to that establishment. The case-type string is named in the source rather than derived from it. The one caveat is that the source is a press release recording two notifications of 5 December 2024 that are not themselves in this corpus.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record the court that has jurisdiction over a SARAS cheque case separately from the place at which the presiding officer is posted.
requirements.why: SARAS cases belong to the jurisdiction of the C.J.M. courts of Ahmedabad City, but the nominated presiding officers sit at Ahmedabad, Anand, Narmada and Gir Somnath and their place of work does not change. A system that derives the court from the officer's station will address summonses, cause lists and certified copies to the wrong district and will report the case under the wrong establishment in the statistics.

binds.target: case record - court of jurisdiction and station of the presiding officer as two fields

requirements.test: Two distinct fields exist; a case whose presiding officer is posted at Narmada still reports its court of jurisdiction as the C.J.M. courts of Ahmedabad City.
requirements.statusReason: Paragraph 4 records that the nominated presiding officers are posted at Ahmedabad, Anand, Narmada and Gir Somnath and that their place of work does not change, paragraph 5 that officers posted anywhere in the State adjudicate cases e-filed in the Ahmedabad City courts, and rule 9.1 that adjudication is valid notwithstanding the remote station. Those passages state a fact about the arrangement; none of them says the court of jurisdiction must be held apart from the officer's station. Separating the two into distinct fields, so that summonses, cause lists and statistics follow the court rather than the officer, is the step taken here, which is why the status was moved off firm.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record whether the complainant in a cheque case is a bank or a Non-Banking Financial Company.
requirements.why: The SARAS establishment was created exclusively for cheque cases instituted by banks and NBFCs; the class of case is defined by who files it as much as by what it is. Without that attribute on the complaint the registry cannot decide at scrutiny whether the case belongs to the SARAS docket or to the ordinary magisterial docket, and an individual payee's complaint can be routed into an establishment that is not open to it.

binds.target: complainant record - institutional class (bank / NBFC / other)

requirements.test: The complainant record carries an institutional-class attribute; SARAS routing is driven by that attribute and rejects a complaint whose complainant is not a bank or an NBFC.
requirements.statusReason: Paragraphs 2 and 3 define the establishment by who files into it, cheque cases e-filed by banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies, and the exclusivity is express. What they describe is the scope of a docket; they say nothing about recording the complainant's institutional class on the complaint. Holding that class as an attribute is what makes the exclusivity testable at scrutiny, and that step is ours rather than the source's, which is why the status was moved off firm.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT treat the physical presence of the presiding officer at the court point as a condition of a valid hearing in a SARAS court.
requirements.why: Rule 9.1 declares adjudication through audio-video electronic means a valid mode notwithstanding that the presiding judicial officer is stationed at a remote location. A workflow that blocks the recording of an order, or marks a hearing irregular, because the officer's location does not match the court's location will stall every SARAS hearing, since by design the officer never sits at Ahmedabad.

binds.target: hearing record - validity of a hearing conducted by audio-video means

requirements.test: A hearing recorded with the presiding officer at a station other than the court's location is accepted and produces a signed order without a warning or override.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 9.1 says that notwithstanding the presiding judicial officers being stationed at remote locations, adjudication in a SARAS Court through audio-video electronic means shall be construed as the valid mode of adjudication. Validity despite the officer's absence from the court point is therefore stated and not read in, and rule 5 of the 2025 rules puts proceedings conducted by video conferencing on the footing of judicial proceedings generally. A workflow treating co-location as a condition would contradict the sub-rule directly.

requirements.statement: The system MUST allow the governing statute of a SARAS case to be recorded as either the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 or the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007.
requirements.why: The SARAS rules apply both to NI Act cheque cases and to e-filed cases under section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, and the definition of 'Act' in rule 2 covers both. A system that hard-codes the NI Act as the only statute for the SARAS docket cannot institute a section 25 case at all, and forces it into the conventional docket where these rules do not apply.

binds.target: case record - governing statute of a SARAS case

requirements.test: Both the NI Act, 1881 and the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 are selectable as the governing statute on a SARAS case, and both route to the same establishment.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 1(c) applies these rules both to the SARAS N.I. Court establishment and to e-filed cases under section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, and rule 2(1)(a) defines 'Act' as the Negotiable Instruments Act and, wherever applicable, the Payment and Settlement Systems Act. Both statutes are named in the text, so the two-statute scope of the docket is stated rather than constructed.

requirements.statement: The system MUST stamp an e-filed complaint with the date and time at which it was electronically received in the Registry, expressed in Indian Standard Time.
requirements.why: The date of e-filing, not the date the advocate assembled the papers or the date of the payment gateway receipt, is what the Gujarat SOP treats as the date of filing. A system that records only a client-side or gateway timestamp cannot show, on a limitation objection, that the complaint reached the Registry inside the period the NI Act allows, and the complaint is liable to be thrown out as time-barred on a record the filer cannot contradict.

binds.target: filing record - receipt timestamp in the Registry

requirements.how: The timestamp is taken when the Action is electronically received in the Registry and is expressed in IST.
requirements.test: The filing record carries a Registry-receipt timestamp in IST that is distinct from any client-side or payment timestamp, and the limitation computation uses only that timestamp.
requirements.statusReason: Clause 14.1 says the date of e-filing will be taken as the date when the Action is electronically received in the Registry, and that Indian Standard Time applies to computing the time at which e-filing is made. The moment that counts and the time zone it is expressed in are both fixed by the clause, so a client-side or gateway stamp is not the filing time on any reading of it.

requirements.statement: The system MUST treat an online e-filing carried out after 1600 hours as filed on the next court working day.
requirements.why: This is the sharpest limitation trap in Gujarat. The portal accepts filings twenty-four hours a day, so a bulk filer uploading a batch at 1830 hours on the last day of the NI Act period believes it is filed in time; the SOP moves that filing to the following working day, which is outside the period. A system that shows the upload date as the filing date will report a whole batch as timely and each of them will be met with a limitation objection.

binds.target: filing record - effective date of filing for limitation

requirements.how: Filing at a Designated Counter is permissible up to 1600 hours on a court working day; an online filing after 1600 hours takes the date which follows, provided that is a court working day.
requirements.test: A complaint uploaded at 1601 hours reports an effective filing date of the next court working day, and the limitation display warns before submission when the cut-off has passed.
requirements.statusReason: Clause 14.2 says that on-line e-filing carried out after 1600 hours on any day will be treated as the date which follows the actual filing date, provided that is a court working day, and permits filing at a Designated Counter up to 1600 hours on a court working day. The cut-off and the roll-forward are stated in terms; clause 14.3 supplies the twenty-four hour availability of the portal that makes the trap possible.

requirements.statement: The system MUST treat a filing made on a gazetted holiday or on a day the court is closed as filed on the next working day.
requirements.why: A bank filing a batch over a long weekend gets an acknowledgement immediately but no filing date until the court reopens. If the system dates the complaint to the upload day, its own limitation arithmetic is a day or more optimistic than the court's, and the error is invisible until the objection is taken.

binds.target: filing record - effective date of filing on a non-working day

requirements.test: A complaint uploaded on a declared holiday reports an effective filing date equal to the next court working day, drawn from the court calendar rather than a generic weekday rule.
requirements.statusReason: Clause 14.2 says that Actions filed on a day declared a gazetted holiday, or on a day when the court is closed, will be regarded as having been filed on the next working day. Both limbs sit in the same sentence, so nothing has to be read in to reach the rule the requirement states.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT offer or record an extension of limitation on the ground that the e-filing portal was unavailable.
requirements.why: The SOP is explicit that no exemption from limitation is permitted for a failure of the web-based e-filing facility; the filer is expected to move to a Designated Counter or to physical filing. A system that presents 'portal down' as a condonation reason teaches bulk filers to rely on a defence that does not exist and delays the fallback to counter filing until the period has run out.

binds.target: limitation screen - reasons available for delay

requirements.test: Portal unavailability is not an available reason for delay anywhere in the limitation workflow; the unavailability path instead surfaces the Designated Counter and physical-filing options.
requirements.statusReason: Clause 14.3 says in terms that no exemption from limitation shall be permitted on the ground of a failure of the web based on-line e-filing facility, and directs the filer instead to a Designated Counter or to physical filing. The prohibition and the fallback are both in the clause, which is why this is a bar on offering the reason at all rather than a caution about relying on it.

requirements.statement: The system MUST compute the court fee on a complaint presented to a criminal court in Gujarat as the fixed amount under Schedule II Article 1(c), independent of the cheque amount.
requirements.why: Gujarat prices a criminal complaint at three rupees whatever the instrument is worth. A system carrying an ad valorem fee model from another state will demand a fee proportionate to the cheque, and a bank filing several thousand cheque cases a year will either over-collect from its own customers or have every filing stopped at scrutiny for a fee that does not match the Schedule.

binds.target: court fee calculation - complaint to a criminal court

requirements.how: Schedule II Article 1(c): three rupees on a writing containing a complaint or charge of any offence presented to any criminal court.
requirements.test: The fee computed for a complaint is the fixed Schedule II Article 1(c) amount and does not vary with the cheque amount across a sample of cases from a few thousand to several crore rupees.
requirements.statusReason: Schedule II Article 1(c) charges three rupees on a writing containing a complaint or charge of any offence presented to any criminal court, a fixed sum with no reference to the value of anything, and section 4 makes payment of the Schedule amount the condition of filing. That the fee does not vary with the cheque follows from the entry sitting in the fixed Schedule at all.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT allow a chargeable document to be filed, exhibited or recorded until the proper fee has been paid.
requirements.why: Section 4 is the gate the registry applies before it numbers a cheque complaint. A system that registers a complaint and only later reconciles the fee produces numbered cases whose filing was void at the outset, and the defect surfaces at the worst moment, when limitation has already run.

binds.target: registration workflow - court fee gate before numbering

requirements.test: Registration of a complaint is blocked until a fee payment of at least the Schedule amount is recorded against it.
requirements.statusReason: Section 4 says that no document of a kind specified as chargeable in the First or Second Schedule shall be filed, exhibited or recorded in any Court of Justice unless the proper fee has been paid. The prohibition names all three acts, so it operates as a gate ahead of the register rather than as an accounting rule applied afterwards.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT prevent a criminal court from filing or exhibiting a document on which the proper fee has not been paid where the presiding judge is of opinion that admission is necessary to prevent a failure of justice.
requirements.why: Section 44 is the safety valve on the criminal side: where the presiding judge is of opinion that filing or exhibition is necessary to prevent a failure of justice, section 4 does not prohibit it. If the fee gate is absolute in software, a short-paid vakalatnama or list of documents can shut out the cheque, the return memo or the demand notice themselves, and the complainant loses the case on an accounting defect rather than on the merits. The section fixes who may open the gate and on what ground; it prescribes no form for doing so, which is why how is left null.

binds.target: exhibit workflow - judicial override of the court fee gate

requirements.test: A presiding-officer role can admit and exhibit a document on which the proper fee has not been paid; the fee gate yields only to that role, and the admission is visible on the case record and in the rojnama.
requirements.statusReason: Section 44 says that where the filing or exhibition in a criminal court of a document on which the proper fee has not been paid is, in the opinion of the Presiding Judge, necessary to prevent a failure of justice, nothing in section 4 shall be deemed to prohibit it. The override, the person who exercises it and the ground are all in the section; only the manner of recording it is left open, which is why how is null.

requirements.statement: The system MUST raise the fixed fee under section 19 when the complainant's first or only examination is reduced to writing and no fee has already been levied on a petition presented by that complainant.
requirements.why: Section 19 attaches a further ten-rupee fee when the examination of a complainant is reduced to writing at the cognizance stage, but it does so on two conditions: the offence must be one for which a police officer may not arrest without a warrant, which a section 138 offence is, and the complainant must not already have presented a petition on which a fee has been levied under the Act. In a cheque case the complaint itself normally bears the Schedule II Article 1(c) fee, so the section 19 fee usually does not attach. A system that raises the fee unconditionally over-collects on every complaint in a bulk batch, and one that never raises it under-collects wherever the complaint carried no fee. The condition, not the amount, is what has to be held on the case.

binds.target: fee ledger - fee raised when the complainant's examination is reduced to writing

requirements.how: Ten rupees under section 19, unless the court thinks fit to remit the payment.
requirements.test: Recording the complainant's examination raises a section 19 fee entry only where no earlier fee-bearing petition by that complainant is on the case; a complaint on which the Article 1(c) fee was levied raises none. The entry can be remitted by the court with the remission recorded.
requirements.statusReason: Section 19 attaches the ten-rupee fee to the first or only examination of a complainant being reduced to writing, and states both conditions the requirement carries: the offence must be one for which a police officer may not arrest without a warrant, and the complainant must not already have presented a petition on which a fee has been levied under the Act. The power to remit sits in the same sentence. The conditions are the section's own, not a gloss placed on it.

requirements.statement: The system MUST require a vakalatnama on record for every pleader appearing for a party, subject to the exceptions the Criminal Manual states.
requirements.why: Bulk cheque filings are run by panel advocates who change between hearings. Without a vakalatnama check at appearance, the record shows submissions and cross-examination conducted by an advocate with no authority on file, and the accused can attack the whole proceeding on that ground at the revision stage.

binds.target: appearance record - vakalatnama required before a pleader is recorded

requirements.how: Rule 135 excepts the Public Prosecutor appearing for Government, a pleader appointed by the court for an accused without means, a pleader appearing as amicus curiae, and a pleader engaged by another duly appointed pleader.
requirements.test: An advocate cannot be attached to a case without a vakalatnama document on record, except under one of the four recorded exceptions.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 135 says vakalatnamas shall be filed by all pleaders appearing on behalf of any party in all classes of cases in all criminal courts in the State, and its proviso lists the four exceptions the requirement carries: the Public Prosecutor for Government, a pleader appointed by the court for an accused without means, a pleader appearing as amicus curiae, and a pleader engaged by another duly appointed pleader. Both the rule and the closed list of exceptions are express.

requirements.statement: The system MUST levy the fixed vakalatnama fee for the level of court to which the vakalatnama is presented.
requirements.why: The fee differs by court: two rupees to a criminal court other than a Sessions Court or the High Court, three rupees to a District or Sessions Court, five rupees to the High Court. A system charging one flat figure across a bulk filer's magistrate, sessions and High Court appearances will short-pay or over-pay every vakalatnama it files at the wrong level.

binds.target: court fee calculation - vakalatnama

requirements.how: Schedule II Article 12: two rupees to a criminal court other than a District Court, Court of Session or the High Court; three rupees to a District or Sessions Court; five rupees to the High Court.
requirements.test: The vakalatnama fee produced for a magistrate's court, a Sessions Court and the High Court differ and match the three Article 12 rates.
requirements.statusReason: Schedule II Article 12 sets three different amounts for a vakalatnama according to the court it is presented to: two rupees to a criminal court other than a District Court, Court of Session or the High Court, three rupees to a District or Sessions Court, and five rupees to the High Court. The rate turning on the level of court is the entry's own structure.

requirements.statement: The system MUST accept payment of court fees by e-payment.
requirements.why: Gujarat amended the Court-Fees Act in 2015 to allow fees to be collected by e-payment, and that is the precondition for e-filing at all. A system that can only record a physical stamp forces a bank filing thousands of complaints on the portal to send a clerk to a treasury for each one, which defeats the whole SARAS design.

binds.target: fee payment - electronic mode

requirements.test: A complaint can be filed end to end with the court fee paid electronically, and the payment reference is stored on the filing record.
requirements.statusReason: Section 37(1) as amended says all fees chargeable under the Act shall be collected by stamps or by e-payment, and section 2(bb) defines e-payment as payment by electronic mode in the manner prescribed. Clause 9 of the e-Filing SOP goes further and requires court fees and other charges to be paid through electronic payment in the manner notified by the High Court. The electronic mode is therefore lawful under the Act and directed by the SOP, so a system confined to a physical stamp is out of step with both.

requirements.statement: The system MUST route all complaints, interlocutory applications, affidavits and pleadings in a SARAS case through the designated e-filing portal.
requirements.why: Rule 4.1 names the portal, and the SARAS rules make reference to the e-Filing SOP mandatory for avoiding objections and defects. A parallel intake path, such as email to the registry or a counter deposit of paper, produces a document that is not on the portal and therefore is not part of the primary judicial record at all.

binds.target: filing intake - the designated e-filing portal

requirements.how: Rule 4.1 names https://filing.ecourts.gov.in/pdedev/ as the designated portal; a person unable to access it may use a designated e-filing counter.
requirements.test: No path exists to create a case document in a SARAS case other than through the portal, a designated e-filing counter, or a Bench exemption recorded under the e-filing exemption requirement; every document on the record carries a portal filing reference or an exemption reference.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 4.1 says all cases, complaints, interlocutory applications, affidavits and other pleadings shall be e-filed through the designated portal, which it names, and rule 4.2 makes reference to the e-Filing SOP mandatory for the avoidance of objections and defects; clause 3.1 of the SOP names the same portal. The obligation is stated, and rule 4.3 supplies the only alternative, a designated e-filing counter for a person unable to access the portal.

requirements.statement: The system MUST present a newly e-filed complaint to the Registry for scrutiny on the next working day after filing.
requirements.why: Rule 4.11 fixes a next-working-day scrutiny. Where a bank uploads a batch of several hundred complaints, a queue without that deadline lets the batch sit unscrutinised while the accused remains unserved and the six-month track clock runs from institution.

binds.target: registry queue - scrutiny due date on a new complaint

requirements.test: Every newly e-filed complaint appears in the Registry scrutiny queue with a due date of the next working day, and the queue reports items past that date.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 4.11 says that upon receipt of a newly e-filed complaint the Registry shall scrutinise the filing on the next working day. The deadline is in the sub-rule and attaches to every new filing, so a queue that carries no due date is not a slower implementation of the rule but a departure from it.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record Registry objections to an e-filed complaint in writing against the filing and communicate them to the e-filer.
requirements.why: An objection conveyed by a phone call or a counter conversation leaves no record of what was wrong or when it was raised. In a bulk filing, the filer cannot tell which of three hundred complaints was objected to, and the rectification cycle stretches until the complaint is out of time on re-presentation.

binds.target: objection record - written objections against an e-filed complaint

requirements.how: The Registry communicates objections by email, SMS or web hosting to the concerned advocate or litigant in person.
requirements.test: Each objection is stored as text against the filing with its date, and the filer receives it on at least one of email, SMS or the portal; the objection history survives after clearance.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 4.11 says that where defects are noticed, objections shall be recorded in writing and communicated for rectification, and clause 18.3 of the SOP names the channels the Registry uses: email, SMS or web hosting to the advocate or litigant in person. The writing and the communication are both directed; clause 2.12 supplies the definition of an objection as a deficiency or error pointed out by the Registry.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT register a complaint under a case type until all Registry objections against it have been cleared.
requirements.why: Rule 4.11 registers the matter only if the filing is found in order or after clearance of all objections. Registration with objections outstanding produces a numbered cheque case whose papers are defective, and the defect resurfaces when the accused takes the point at the framing or plea stage, by which time the complaint cannot be refiled within time.

binds.target: registration workflow - objection clearance gate

requirements.test: Registration is blocked while any objection against the filing is open; clearing the last objection makes registration available.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 4.11 registers the matter under the appropriate case type if the filing is found in order, and otherwise only upon clearance of all objections. Registration after clearance is the sub-rule's own sequence, so a numbered case with objections still open is not a permissible variant of it.

requirements.statement: The system MUST restrict scrutiny of e-filed complaints and documents for technical compliance to users holding a Registry role.
requirements.why: Rule 3.10 keeps technical scrutiny within the exclusive domain of the Registry. If a bench clerk or the presiding officer's own staff can clear defects, the separation between the ministerial gate and the judicial record breaks down, and a case can reach the presiding officer having never been checked by the office answerable for it.

binds.target: scrutiny function - restricted to the Registry role

requirements.test: A user without the Registry role cannot record, clear or waive a technical-compliance objection; the attempt is refused and logged.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 3.10 says scrutiny of e-filed complaints and documents for technical compliance shall remain within the exclusive domain of the Registry. The word exclusive is what turns this from an allocation of work into a restriction, so treating it as an access rule follows the sub-rule rather than extending it.

requirements.statement: The system SHOULD reject an online e-file whose size exceeds twenty megabytes and direct the filer to a Designated Counter.
requirements.why: The Gujarat SOP says the size of an e-file should not exceed twenty megabytes and that a filer whose file is larger should visit a Designated Counter; it directs rather than commands, which is why this is a SHOULD. Cheque-case bundles carrying scanned statements of account and a long series of return memos routinely exceed that. A system that lets the upload begin and fails at the end wastes the filer's cut-off window, and on the last day of the NI Act period that is the difference between a filed and a time-barred complaint.

binds.target: upload control - twenty megabyte ceiling on an online e-file

requirements.test: An e-file over twenty megabytes is refused before upload starts, with the Designated Counter route offered in the same message.
requirements.statusReason: Clause 3.4 says the size of the e-file should not exceed twenty megabytes and that where it does, the advocate or litigant should visit a Designated Counter to file through the intranet. Both the ceiling and the fallback are in the clause, and the requirement's SHOULD tracks the clause's own should. What the clause does not say is who enforces the ceiling; applying it at the portal rather than leaving it to the filer is an implementation choice and not an addition to the norm.

requirements.statement: The system MUST produce every e-filed document as an OCR-searchable PDF, with OCR enablement for Gujarati text.
requirements.why: The record of a Gujarat cheque case is routinely part Gujarati. A scanned image PDF without a Gujarati OCR layer cannot be searched by the presiding officer, cannot be indexed for exhibit assignment, and defeats the purpose of making the electronic record the primary judicial record.

binds.target: document conversion - OCR-searchable PDF, PDF/A preferred

requirements.how: PDF/A is the preferred format; a non-text document is scanned at 300 dpi in OCR-searchable mode. Local-language text uses LOHIT Gujarati Unicode font 13.
requirements.test: A document uploaded without a text layer is refused; a Gujarati document uploaded through the workflow yields searchable Gujarati text.
requirements.statusReason: Clause 6.2 requires the document to be converted into an OCR searchable PDF or PDF/A including OCR enablement for Gujarati fonts, and names PDF/A as the preferred format; clause 6.3 fixes 300 dpi in OCR searchable mode for a document that is not a text document, and SARAS rule 3.7 requires physically produced documents to be scanned and OCR-enabled before they reach the record. The Gujarati OCR layer is named in the clause itself rather than inferred from the language of the record.

requirements.statement: The system MUST prepare every e-filed document in A4 size except where the original paper size does not permit it.
requirements.why: Both the SOP formatting clause and SARAS rule 4.8 fix A4. A bundle mixing legal and A4 pages breaks pagination in the merged PDF, which in turn breaks the exhibit and bookmark references that the rojnama and the certified copy depend on.

binds.target: document conversion - page size

requirements.test: Generated and converted documents are A4; a non-A4 page is flagged at upload with the original-size exception available and recorded.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 4.8 says that except where the original size of the paper does not permit compliance, all documents, whether scanned or directly converted into PDF, shall be prepared in A4 size, and clause 6.1 of the SOP fixes A-4 for original typed material. The rule and its single exception are both express.

requirements.statement: The system MUST reject a filing whose document file name uses a disallowed character or exceeds forty-five characters including spaces.
requirements.why: The SOP lists the characters a document binary file name may not contain and caps the name at forty-five characters. An institutional filer generating names automatically from a loan account reference will produce names with slashes, ampersands and hundreds of characters, and the whole batch is bounced at the counter for a reason nothing on the screen explained.

binds.target: upload control - document file name

requirements.how: Disallowed characters: quotation mark, number sign, per cent, ampersand, asterisk, colon, angle brackets, question mark, backslash, forward slash, braces, pipe, tilde, and a period used consecutively or at the start or end of the name.
requirements.test: A file named with any listed character, or longer than forty-five characters, is refused at selection with the offending character named.
requirements.statusReason: Clause 8.6 lists the special characters that are not allowed in a document binary file name, ending with the period used consecutively in the middle of the name or at its start or end, and says file names should not exceed forty-five characters in length including spaces. The list and the cap are the clause's own, and the requirement carries them without extension.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT submit an e-filed document that is watermarked, encrypted, or carries markings, track changes or annotations.
requirements.why: The SOP forbids all of these on an e-filing. A bank's document management system commonly stamps a confidentiality watermark and password-protects statements as a matter of policy; if that reaches the portal the filing is defective and the defect is invisible to the person uploading it.

binds.target: upload control - document hygiene

requirements.test: An encrypted PDF, a PDF with tracked changes, and a PDF with annotation objects are each refused at upload with the reason stated.
requirements.statusReason: Clause 8.7 says on-line e-filing shall not be watermarked or encrypted, and that all e-filed documents shall be legible and free of markings, track changes or annotations. Every item the requirement forbids appears in that clause.

requirements.statement: The system MUST merge the text and scanned documents of a filing into a single OCR-searchable PDF bookmarked in accordance with the Master Index approved by the Registry.
requirements.why: Bookmarking to the Master Index is what lets the Registry, and later the presiding officer, find the cheque, the return memo and the notice inside a hundred-page bundle. A filing uploaded as a heap of separate unbookmarked files is objected to at scrutiny, and in a bulk batch that objection repeats across every case in the batch.

binds.target: filing bundle - merged bookmarked PDF

requirements.test: The submitted bundle is one PDF whose bookmark tree matches the Master Index, and each bookmark resolves to the correct first page.
requirements.statusReason: Clause 8.1 says the text documents and scanned documents should be merged as a single OCR searchable PDF file and should be book-marked as per the Master Index duly approved by the Registry, and clause 8.2 makes the merged document the thing that is uploaded. The single file, the OCR layer and the Master Index bookmarking are all named in the clause.

requirements.statement: The system MUST upload a document that originates in electronic form directly, without scanning it.
requirements.why: Rule 4.5 confines scanning to documents that inherently originate in physical form. A bank that prints an electronically generated statement of account in order to scan it destroys the text layer, produces a larger file that risks the twenty megabyte ceiling, and reduces a natively authentic document to an image whose authenticity can be questioned.

binds.target: document intake - native electronic documents

requirements.test: The filing workflow distinguishes natively electronic documents from physical originals and offers no scan step for the former.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 4.5 says documents inherently originating in physical form shall alone be scanned and uploaded, and that documents originating in electronic form shall be uploaded directly; rule 4.6 prefers direct generation in PDF for complaints, vakalatnamas, lists of documents, affidavits and applications. The word alone is what closes the scanning route for a natively electronic document, so the prohibition is in the text.

requirements.statement: The system MUST notify the filing or registration number to the e-filer once the e-filing is accepted.
requirements.why: Without a number returned to the filer, an institutional filer cannot reconcile a batch of uploads against its own case management records, and a complaint that silently failed to register is indistinguishable from one that succeeded until the limitation period has passed.

binds.target: filing acknowledgement - number returned to the filer

requirements.test: Acceptance of an e-filing returns a filing or registration number to the filer's account and by the notification channel on record.
requirements.statusReason: Clause 8.3 says that once e-filing is accepted, the filing or registration number shall be notified to the advocate or litigant in person. The notification is directed and its addressee named, so nothing is read in.

requirements.statement: The system MAY record an exemption from e-filing granted by the Bench on an application stating one of the permitted grounds.
requirements.why: The SOP permits exemption where e-filing is not feasible, where confidentiality or privacy is in issue, where the document cannot be scanned because of its size, shape or condition, where the portal is unavailable, or for just and sufficient cause. A cheque case can involve an instrument in a condition that will not scan; with no way to record the exemption the document simply never enters the record.

binds.target: exemption record - Bench order exempting a document from e-filing

requirements.test: An exemption can be applied for, granted by a judicial role against one of the five listed grounds, and is visible on the case record against the document it covers.
requirements.statusReason: Clause 12 says exemption from on-line e-filing of the entire pleading or a part of the pleadings or documents may be permitted by the Bench upon an application, and lists the five circumstances the requirement carries, ending with just and sufficient cause. The permission, the application that triggers it and the grounds are all in the clause, and the level is MAY because the clause is permissive on its face.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record service as deemed effected where a summons sent by digitally signed electronic communication is acknowledged within five working days.
requirements.why: Service is the single biggest cause of delay in a Gujarat cheque case. Rule 5(iv) makes digitally signed electronic communication a preferential mode with deemed service on acknowledgement; the deeming reaches a criminal trial through rule 21(B), which applies the same norms to criminal trials with the changes the Code requires. A system that treats an acknowledged e-summons as merely informal keeps the case in the bailiff queue for months after service was in law complete.

binds.target: service record - deemed service by acknowledged e-communication

requirements.how: Service is deemed made on acknowledgement of receipt by the other side, the acknowledgement being within five working days.
requirements.test: An acknowledged digitally signed e-summons sets the service status to served with the acknowledgement date stored; the five-working-day window is computed on court working days.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 5(iv) makes service through digitally signed electronic communication an additional and preferential mode, and says that upon acknowledgement of receipt by the other side, the acknowledgement being within five working days, the service shall be deemed to have been made in accordance with the requirements of the Code. The deeming is express. What is not is the reach: rule 5 is written for a suit, appeal or original proceeding, and it touches a criminal complaint only through rule 21(B), which applies the same norms with the corresponding changes required by the Code of Criminal Procedure. That carry is the inference.

requirements.statement: The system MUST require an affidavit of service on the record where service of summons is effected by the complainant or by a certified or registered courier.
requirements.why: Institutional cheque filers serve through their own courier arrangements as a matter of course. Rule 5(v) makes the affidavit of service the proof, and without it on the record the court cannot proceed against an absent accused; the complainant loses the hearing and the case is adjourned for the affidavit that should have accompanied the return.

binds.target: service record - affidavit of service for complainant or courier service

requirements.test: A service return entered as complainant service or courier service cannot be accepted without an affidavit-of-service document attached.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 5(v) says that in cases where service of summons is permitted and is effected by the plaintiff or a certified or registered courier, the concerned person shall file an affidavit of service in the prescribed manner, form and time. The direction is express on the civil side. Its application to a complainant serving an accused in a cheque case runs through rule 21(B) rather than through the words of rule 5, and that step is why the status is inferred.

requirements.statement: The system MUST require a signed declaration verifying a return of refusal made by the complainant or by a courier agency.
requirements.why: Rule 5(vi) requires the return endorsed 'refused' to be accompanied by a declaration signed by the complainant or a responsible person of the courier agency that the endorsement is correct, on pain of perjury. A refusal accepted without it cannot support an ex parte order, and the accused reopens the proceeding years later on the ground that he was never served.

binds.target: service record - declaration supporting a refusal endorsement

requirements.how: The declaration states that the endorsement made is correct and acknowledges that a false endorsement is punishable for perjury or as an abuse of the Code.
requirements.test: A return with outcome 'refused' cannot be saved without an attached signed declaration naming the declarant and his capacity.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 5(vi) requires a return endorsed as refused to be accompanied by a declaration, signed by the plaintiff or by a responsible person of the courier agency, that the endorsement made is correct, with the declarant exposed to punishment for perjury or summary treatment for abuse of the Code if it is false; it is on consideration of that declaration that the court may place the defendant ex parte. The declaration and its content are stated. What is read in is the transposition to a criminal complaint through rule 21(B).

requirements.statement: The system SHOULD prevent a black-listed courier agency from being selected to effect service.
requirements.why: Rule 5(vi) allows a courier agency to be black-listed for a false endorsement of refusal. The rule states the consequence but not the machinery; the system consequence is inferred. If the black-list exists only on a circular, a bulk filer with a national courier contract will keep serving through a black-listed agency, and every one of those returns is open to attack.

binds.target: service record - courier agency selection

requirements.test: A courier agency marked black-listed is not selectable on a new service instruction, and existing instructions to it are reported.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 5(vi) says only that where the person concerned was representing a certified or registered courier agency, that agency can be black-listed. It creates a consequence and names nobody who must keep the list, publish it, or act on it when a courier is next chosen. Turning it into a control at the point of selection is our reading of what a black-list is for, and the level is SHOULD because the rule leaves the consequence itself discretionary.

requirements.statement: The system MUST order issue of summons through the bailiff and substituted service simultaneously when a summons sent by post or courier is reported unserved.
requirements.why: Rule 5(vii) is emphatic that the two go out together. The common practice of trying bailiff service first and only then applying for substituted service adds a full cycle of six to eight weeks to a cheque case that is meant to conclude in six months, and it is exactly the pattern a workflow that offers the two steps in sequence will produce.

binds.target: service escalation - simultaneous bailiff and substituted service

requirements.test: Recording a postal or courier return of non-service raises a single escalation action that creates both a bailiff process and a substituted service process; neither can be created alone from that trigger.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 5(vii) says that whenever a summons or notice issued to a defendant or respondent through post or courier is reported unserved, the Court shall order issuance of summons through bailiff and substituted service simultaneously. The simultaneity is in the word the rule uses and is not read in. The inference is the reach again: the sub-rule speaks of a defendant or respondent, and it governs a criminal complaint only through rule 21(B).

requirements.statement: The system MUST list a case for dismissal for non-prosecution where the process fee for service is not paid within three days of the order.
requirements.why: Rule 5(iii) attaches a three-day clock to the process fee, and rule 21(B) carries it to the criminal side. A bank filing in bulk pays process fees on a monthly reconciliation cycle; without this clock exposed on the case, the first the filer learns of the default is when its complaint appears on the dismissal list.

binds.target: process fee - three day clock and dismissal listing

requirements.test: An order for process starts a three-day fee clock on the case; on expiry without payment the case appears on the non-prosecution cause list and the filer is notified.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 5(iii) says the process fee for service shall be paid within three days from the date of the order, failing which the case will be posted in Cause List-I for dismissal for non-prosecution. The clock and the consequence are both express, and rule 21(B) is what carries them to a criminal proceeding. That carry, together with treating the listing as something the record must surface to the filer rather than an act done quietly in the office, is why the status is inferred.

requirements.statement: The system MUST price each process issued in a cheque case according to the current table of process fees published for the court.
requirements.why: The process fee is charged per process, and differently for a summons, a warrant of arrest, a proclamation and a warrant of attachment; section 33 requires the table of the fees chargeable for service and execution to be exposed to view in a conspicuous part of every court, which makes the published table and not a figure in code the source of the rate. A system carrying a single hard-coded process fee will under-recover on the warrant stage of every contested cheque case. Two cautions on the rate: the figures in Criminal Manual rule 41 are the 1977 table, made under section 32 of the repealed Bombay Court Fees Act, 1959; and the corresponding rule-making power in section 32 of the Gujarat Court-Fees Act, 2004 was itself deleted by Gujarat 14 of 2016, so the current rates must be taken from the table published for the court and not reconstructed from rule 41.

binds.target: fee ledger - process fee per process type

requirements.how: Rule 41 charges a distinct fee for every summons or notice, every warrant of arrest, every proclamation and every warrant of attachment; no fee is levied on a process issued on the complaint of a police officer acting as such, nor on the re-issue of a process; and the court may remit the process fees in whole or in part where the complainant or the accused has not the means to pay them.
requirements.test: Issuing a summons, a warrant of arrest, a proclamation and a warrant of attachment each raise a distinct fee entry at the rate held for that process type, and the rate table is editable without a code change.
requirements.statusReason: Section 33 requires a table showing the fees chargeable for service and execution to be exposed to view in a conspicuous part of each court. That is a duty to display a table; the section neither says that a fee is charged per process nor fixes any rate. Rule 41 does set a distinct fee for every summons, warrant of arrest, proclamation and warrant of attachment, but it was made under section 32 of the repealed Bombay Court Fees Act, 1959, and the corresponding rule-making power in section 32 of the 2004 Act was deleted by Gujarat 14 of 2016, so its table cannot be taken as the rate in force. Reading the two together to require pricing per process type from a table held as data is our construction, which is why the status was moved off firm.

requirements.statement: The system MUST state on a process issued to a witness who is to be examined by video conferencing the date, time and venue of the designated place, and direct the witness to attend in person with proof of identity.
requirements.why: In a cheque case the witness summoned this way is usually the bank officer who proves the dishonour. A summons that gives only a hearing date and no designated place leaves the officer with nowhere to go; he attends his own branch, the deposition does not happen, and the return memo goes unproved for another hearing.

binds.target: witness summons for video conferencing - designated place and identity direction

requirements.how: The process states the date, time and venue of the concerned designated place and directs the witness to attend in person along with proof of identity.
requirements.test: A witness summons generated for a video-conferencing examination carries a designated place with its address, the time, and the identity direction; it cannot be generated without a designated place selected.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 12 says that processes issued to a witness who is to be examined through video conferencing shall mention the date, time and venue of the concerned designated place, and shall direct the witness to attend in person along with proof of identity. Every element the requirement puts on the face of the process is named in that sentence, and rule 6 supplies what counts as proof of identity.

requirements.statement: The system MUST accompany a process issued to a witness with a copy of any document with reference to which the witness is to be examined.
requirements.why: Rule 12 requires the document to travel with the process. A bank officer summoned to prove a return memo he has not seen since it was generated cannot depose to it from memory; the examination collapses and has to be listed again, and the cheque case loses a hearing over a missing enclosure.

binds.target: witness summons - enclosed copy of the document of examination

requirements.test: Where a witness is linked to one or more documents on the case, the generated process packet includes copies of exactly those documents.
requirements.statusReason: The second sentence of rule 12 says that if a person is examined with reference to a particular document, the process to the witness must be accompanied by a copy of the document. The enclosure is directed in terms, and the condition that triggers it, examination with reference to a document, is the rule's own.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT treat service by a Registry official's designated e-mail address as a substitute for the prescribed mode of service.
requirements.why: Clause 13 makes electronic service by Registry e-mail an addition to the prescribed mode, not a replacement, and publishes the Registry e-mail IDs on the court website only so that a recipient can verify the source. A system that closes the service task when the Registry e-mail is sent will show an accused as served who has not been served in law, and the ex parte order that follows will not survive a challenge. The clause prescribes no method for keeping the two apart, so how is null.

binds.target: service record - status of electronic service by the Registry

requirements.test: Dispatch by Registry e-mail is recorded as an additional service event and does not by itself move the accused's service status to served.
requirements.statusReason: Clause 13 opens with the words 'In addition to the prescribed mode of service' and then permits notices, documents and pleadings filed electronically also to be served through the designated e-mail IDs of Registry officials, which are published on the court website so that a recipient can verify the source. The clause adds a channel and expressly does not displace the prescribed mode, so closing the service task on a Registry e-mail would contradict its opening words. It prescribes no method for keeping the two apart, which is why how is null.

requirements.statement: The system MUST identify on the face of a process served through the police the court that issued it and the authentication under which it was issued.
requirements.why: The police officer's duty under section 64(a) is to serve promptly every summons and execute every warrant lawfully issued to him by a competent authority. A digitally issued process that does not show its issuing court and authentication gives the constable no basis to act on it, and in a SARAS case, where the presiding officer sits in another district, that objection is easy to raise and hard to answer. The Act imposes the duty on the officer and the requirement on the document is inferred from what the duty attaches to.

binds.target: process for police service - issuing court and authentication

requirements.test: A printed or transmitted process shows the issuing court, the presiding officer's digital signature and a verifiable reference back to the portal record.
requirements.statusReason: Section 64(a) makes it the duty of every police officer promptly to serve every summons and obey and execute every warrant or other order lawfully issued to him by a competent authority. The duty falls on the officer, and the only qualifier is that the process be lawfully issued by a competent authority; the section says nothing about what a process must show on its face. Rule 4.18 requires orders to be generated in PDF and digitally signed by the Presiding Officer, but not that the issuing court and the authentication be legible to the constable holding the paper. Putting them there is the step that makes the officer's duty capable of being discharged, and it is ours.

requirements.statement: The system MUST accept the examination-in-chief of a complainant's witness as an affidavit tendered through electronic filing.
requirements.why: Rule 6.1 makes the affidavit through the portal the ordinary mode in a SARAS cheque case. A workflow that can only record oral chief examination in the courtroom forces every bank officer to travel to a physical court, which is precisely the cost the remote-adjudication design exists to remove, and the six-month track limit will not survive it.

binds.target: evidence recording - chief examination tendered by e-filed affidavit

requirements.test: A chief-examination affidavit can be e-filed against a named witness, exhibited, and closed as the chief examination without any physical hearing event.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 6.1 says the examination-in-chief of witnesses for the complainant shall ordinarily be tendered by way of affidavit through electronic filing. The mode is directed rather than merely permitted, and ordinarily marks the exception rather than weakening the rule. What makes the affidavit lawful in the first place is section 145(1) as read in Mandvi Cooperative Bank and applied in the Indian Bank Association directions; rule 6.1 is Gujarat routing that established mode through the portal.

requirements.statement: The system MUST schedule cross-examination, the examination-in-chief of the accused and the evidence of a defence witness for physical presence before the court, at a notified Formal Witness Deposition Centre, or at a notified Remote Point.
requirements.why: Rule 6.2 keeps these physical by default. A system that defaults every evidence event to a video link will list cross-examination remotely without the judicial permission rule 6.3 requires, and the resulting deposition is open to attack on the ground that it was recorded in a mode the rules do not allow as the ordinary course.

binds.target: evidence scheduling - venue for cross-examination and defence evidence

requirements.how: The venue is the court, a Formal Witness Deposition Centre notified by the High Court and published on its website, or a Remote Point Location notified by the Government.
requirements.test: Scheduling a cross-examination requires a venue chosen from the court, a notified FWDC or a notified Remote Point; a video-conferencing venue requires the permission recorded under the audio-video requirement.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 6.2 says the examination-in-chief of the accused, the witness for the accused and cross-examination of witnesses shall ordinarily be conducted by physical presence before the Court, at a Formal Witness Deposition Centre notified by the High Court, or at a Remote Point Location notified by the Government. The three events and the three venues are both listed in the sub-rule. The asymmetry against rule 6.1 is not accidental: Mandvi Cooperative Bank holds that section 145(1) lets the complainant depose on affidavit and does not extend the same to the accused.

requirements.statement: The system MUST store on the case record the court's permission before evidence is recorded by audio-video electronic means.
requirements.why: Rule 6.3 makes audio-video recording of evidence a matter of judicial discretion exercised under the 2025 rules. If the permission is not on the record, the deposition looks on its face like an ordinary remote hearing, and on appeal there is nothing to show the discretion was exercised at all.

binds.target: evidence record - judicial permission for audio-video recording

requirements.test: An evidence event with an audio-video venue carries a reference to the order permitting it; without that reference the event cannot be marked complete.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 6.3 says recording of evidence through audio-video electronic means may be permitted subject to judicial discretion, strictly in accordance with the 2025 rules. The permission is a condition of using the mode at all, so a deposition recorded that way without it is recorded contrary to the sub-rule. Holding the permission on the record is the record of compliance with an express precondition rather than a precondition of our own.

requirements.statement: The system MUST retain the original cheque, return memo and demand notice in physical custody for the duration of the trial notwithstanding that they have been scanned and e-filed.
requirements.why: The Gujarat e-Filing SOP lists the documents to be preserved permanently and expressly excludes a cheque from the negotiable instruments in that list. SARAS rule 3.11 closes the gap: the originals are retained during trial for evidentiary purposes. A system that treats the scan as the whole record and releases the physical bundle at registration leaves the complainant unable to produce the instrument when the accused disputes the signature, which is the one issue on which a cheque case is actually fought.

binds.target: document record - physical custody status of the original instrument

requirements.how: After trial the originals are preserved and dealt with in accordance with final judicial directions, or until the dispute attains finality in appeal or revision.
requirements.test: Each of the cheque, return memo and demand notice carries a physical-custody status; the case cannot be marked ready for evidence while any of them is recorded as neither in court custody nor returned on endorsement.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 3.11 says original cheques and other documents produced physically, though excluded from permanent preservation under the Gujarat e-Filing SOP, shall be retained during trial for evidentiary purposes, and shall thereafter be preserved and dealt with in accordance with final judicial directions or until the dispute attains finality in appeal or revision. Clause 10.3 is the exclusion it refers to, its permanent-preservation list reaching a negotiable instrument other than a cheque. Retention through trial is stated in the sub-rule and is not read into the SOP's silence.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record an endorsement naming the case number, the exhibit number and the date when an original document is returned to the complainant.
requirements.why: Rule 3.9 permits the cheque, return memo, notice, bills and invoices to go back to the complainant on request, on condition of producing them whenever ordered and on that endorsement. Without the endorsement stored against the exhibit, the record shows an exhibit with no document behind it and no trace of who holds it, and the court cannot recall the instrument when the accused finally disputes it.

binds.target: return of original - endorsement on the returned document

requirements.how: The endorsement reads that the document is produced in Case No. ____ at Exhibit No. ____ dated ____, and the return is conditional on the complainant producing the document whenever ordered to do so.
requirements.test: Returning an original requires the case number, exhibit number and date; the generated endorsement carries all three and the exhibit shows the document as returned with the holder recorded.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 3.9 permits the original cheque, return memo, notice, bills and invoices produced physically to be returned to the complainant on request, on condition of producing them to the court whenever ordered, and with an endorsement that such document is produced in Case No. ____ at exhibit No. _____ dated ____. The three particulars the requirement demands are the blanks in the rule's own form of endorsement.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record the sealed cover marking, carrying the case particulars, for every document produced or signed physically in a SARAS case.
requirements.why: Rules 3.8 and 3.12 require physically signed originals and physically produced documents to be kept in sealed and appropriately marked covers, marked with the particulars of the case they belong to. In a remote-adjudication court where the presiding officer is in another district, an unmarked cover cannot be matched back to a case at all, and the bundle is found only by opening every envelope in the room.

binds.target: document record - sealed cover marking

requirements.how: The Bench Clerk or other designated ministerial staff places the physically produced documents of each case file in a sealed envelope duly marked with the case particulars.
requirements.test: Every physically held document carries a cover marking bearing the case particulars, and a query by case number returns the marking of the cover holding that case's documents.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 3.8 requires physically signed originals, once scanned and uploaded, to be preserved in sealed and appropriately marked covers in the custody of the court staff, and rule 3.12 requires the Bench Clerk or other designated ministerial staff to place the physically produced documents of each case file in a sealed envelope duly marked with the case particulars. Both the sealing and what the marking must carry are stated.

requirements.statement: The system MUST preserve the signed vakalatnama, a notarised or attested affidavit, and any document whose authenticity is likely to be questioned, for at least two years after final disposal including disposal by the superior appellate court.
requirements.why: Clause 10.2 of the e-Filing SOP fixes the retention floor, and SARAS rule 13.2 sends retention of originals back to it. A cheque whose signature is disputed is exactly a document whose authenticity is likely to be questioned. A retention clock that starts at trial-court judgment will destroy the original while the appeal is still alive.

binds.target: retention record - two year floor running from final disposal

requirements.test: The retention clock for these classes of document starts at final disposal including appellate disposal, not at trial judgment, and no destruction action is available before the floor expires.
requirements.statusReason: Clause 10.2 says the signed vakalatnama, the signed and notarized or attested affidavit, and any other document whose authenticity is likely to be questioned, should be preserved at least for two years till after the final disposal of the Action, and adds in the next sentence that final disposal shall include disposal by the superior appellate court. SARAS rule 13.2 adopts clause 10 for retention of originals in a SARAS case. Both the floor and the event it runs from are express.

requirements.statement: The system MUST attribute the responsibility for producing the original and proving its genuineness to the party that electronically filed the scanned copy.
requirements.why: Clause 10.4 places that duty on the e-filer. Where a bank's panel advocate uploads the scan and the bank holds the original in a branch strong room, nobody on the record is named as answerable for it. When the court calls for the instrument, the advocate points at the bank and the bank at the advocate, and the case is adjourned while the cheque is traced.

binds.target: document record - party answerable for the original

requirements.test: Each scanned document records the filing party, and a call for the original is addressed to that party by name.
requirements.statusReason: Clause 10.4 says the responsibility of producing the originals and proving their genuineness shall be of the party that has electronically filed scanned copies of the document. The allocation is the clause's own; what the requirement adds is only that the record hold the filing party by name, so that a call for the original has an addressee.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record an undertaking by the person uploading a scanned document that the physical original will be preserved in its original condition until produced before the court or dealt with under judicial directions.
requirements.why: The proviso to rule 4.10 makes the scanned document the record of the court notwithstanding that the original stays with the person producing it, and puts on every person uploading a scanned PDF the duty to ensure that the corresponding physical original is preserved in its original condition until produced on demand or dealt with under judicial directions. The proviso states the duty; that the duty be captured as a recorded undertaking at the moment of upload is the reading and not the text, which is why this is inferred. In a bulk filing the originals are warehoused by the filer; without the undertaking captured at upload there is no recorded obligation on any named person to keep them intact, and a cheque returned to a recovery agent for parallel civil action is gone from the criminal case.

binds.target: filing record - undertaking to preserve the physical original

requirements.test: Uploading a scanned document requires the undertaking to be affirmed, and the affirmation with its actor and timestamp is stored on the document record.
requirements.statusReason: The proviso to rule 4.10 puts on every person uploading scanned PDF documents the duty to ensure that the corresponding physical originals are preserved in their original condition until produced before the Court on demand or dealt with in accordance with judicial directions, and the body of the sub-rule makes the scanned document the record of the Court notwithstanding that the original stays with the person producing it. The duty and the person who bears it are both stated. What the proviso does not do is require it to be captured as an undertaking affirmed at the moment of upload; making it a recorded act with an actor and a timestamp is the step taken here, and it is why this is inferred.

requirements.statement: The system MUST support each of the prescribed modes of showing a document to a person being examined at a remote point.
requirements.why: A cheque case is fought over three documents. If the only way to put the cheque to a remote witness is to read it out, the examination is worthless. Rule 14 sets out exactly how the document travels in each direction, and a video platform without a document channel cannot comply.

binds.target: remote examination - showing a document to the person examined

requirements.how: Where the document is at the Court Point, by document visualizer, or if none is available by transmitting a copy or image through the designated video conferencing software or official e-mail; where the document is at the remote point, by transmitting a copy or image to the Court Point.
requirements.test: All three modes are available during a remote examination, and the document transmitted is logged against the examination event.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 14 enumerates the ways a document may be shown to a person examined at a remote point: by document visualizer where the document is at the Court Point, by transmitting a copy or image through the designated video conferencing software or official e-mail where no visualizer is available, and by transmitting a copy or image to the Court Point where the document is at the remote point. The modes are listed in the rule, so supporting each of them follows its terms rather than extending them.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record the dispatch to the Court Point of the hard copy of a document held at the remote point, countersigned by the witness and by the coordinator at the designated place.
requirements.why: Rule 14(c) requires the paper copy to follow the transmitted image. If only the image reaches the record, the document the witness actually looked at and signed is nowhere in the file, and its identity can be disputed on appeal.

binds.target: remote examination - dispatch of the countersigned hard copy

requirements.test: An examination on a document held at the remote point cannot be closed without a dispatch entry for the countersigned hard copy.
requirements.statusReason: The last sentence of rule 14(c) says the hard copy of the document, countersigned by the witness and by the coordinator at the designated place, shall also be dispatched to the Court Point. The word also is what makes the paper copy an addition to the transmitted image rather than an alternative to it, and both countersignatures are named in the rule.

requirements.statement: The system MUST place on the judicial record the transcript of a remotely recorded examination, read over and explained to the person examined and bearing that person's signature.
requirements.why: Rule 13(3) makes the signed transcript part of the record, and prescribes both a digital and a print-and-scan route depending on what is available at the remote point. A system that stores only the video recording or an unsigned machine transcript produces evidence the accused can refuse to be bound by, and the bank officer has to be recalled.

binds.target: deposition transcript from a remote examination

requirements.how: Where digital signatures exist at both points, the transcript digitally signed by the presiding officer goes to the remote coordinator, is printed and signed by the person examined, and the scanned copy digitally signed by the coordinator returns to the Court Point. Where they do not, the printout signed by the presiding judge is sent in non-editable scanned form, signed by the person examined and countersigned by the coordinator, and returned to the Court Point where a printout is taken onto the record.
requirements.test: A remote examination cannot be closed without a signed transcript on the record; both prescribed routes are available and the route used is recorded.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 13(3) says the Court shall read over and explain the evidence recorded to the witness, obtain the signature of the person being examined on the transcript immediately after the examination concludes, and that the signed transcript shall form part of the record of the judicial proceedings. Clauses (a) and (b) then prescribe the two routes for obtaining that signature according to whether digital signatures exist at both points. The obligation and both alternatives are in the sub-rule.

requirements.statement: The system MUST head an affidavit used in a Gujarat criminal court in the form the Criminal Manual prescribes.
requirements.why: The chief examination in a SARAS cheque case is tendered as an affidavit, and a bulk filer generates those from a template. A template with the wrong heading produces the same defect on every affidavit in a batch, and each is objected to at scrutiny.

binds.target: affidavit template - heading and title

requirements.how: The heading is 'In the Court ........ at ........' naming the court. Where a case is pending it also begins with 'In the matter of case of ........'; where no case is pending, 'In the matter of the application of ........'.
requirements.test: An affidavit generated by the system carries the court heading and the matter heading, populated from the case record.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 236 fixes the heading of every affidavit to be used in a court of law as 'In the Court........at......' naming the court, requires it, where a case is pending, also to begin with 'In the matter of case of........', and where no case is pending, with 'In the matter of the application of........'. The forms of words are the rule's own.

requirements.statement: The system MUST draw an affidavit in the first person and in consecutively numbered paragraphs, each confined as far as may be to a distinct subject.
requirements.why: Rule 237 governs the form. A chief-examination affidavit generated as continuous prose cannot be cross-examined paragraph by paragraph, and the court cannot record which averment was put to the witness; the deposition becomes hard to use in the judgment.

binds.target: affidavit template - paragraphing and person

requirements.test: A generated affidavit is in the first person with consecutively numbered paragraphs, and the numbering is stable when the affidavit is exhibited.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 237 says every affidavit shall be drawn up in the first person and divided into paragraphs numbered consecutively, each paragraph, as far as may be, confined to a distinct subject or portion of one. Both the person and the paragraphing are directed by the rule in terms.

requirements.statement: The system MUST require the chief-examination affidavit of a witness to be on record before that witness is listed for evidence.
requirements.why: Rule 9(5) requires the parties to keep the affidavit in chief examination ready whenever the witness's examination is taken up, and rule 9(4) requires evidence to run day to day with all witnesses in attendance; rule 21(B) carries both to a criminal trial. Listing a bank witness without his affidavit on file guarantees an adjournment, and in a case with a six-month outer limit a handful of such adjournments consumes the whole allowance.

binds.target: cause list - witness listing precondition

requirements.test: A witness without a chief-examination affidavit on record cannot be added to an evidence listing, and the block names the missing affidavit.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 9(5) says the parties shall keep the affidavit in chief-examination ready whenever the witness's examination is taken up, and rule 9(4) that evidence must as far as possible be recorded day to day with all witnesses in attendance. Keeping an affidavit ready is a duty on the party at the hearing; neither sub-rule says the affidavit must be on the record before the witness can be listed at all, and both are written for a civil trial, reaching a criminal complaint through rule 21(B). Turning the readiness duty into a listing precondition is the reading taken here.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record the named custodian holding the physical documents of a SARAS case.
requirements.why: Rule 13.1 places physical documents in the custody of the Superintendent or Board Clerk or as the Presiding Officer of the Court decides, and rule 3.12 requires them to be maintained so as to ensure ready and prompt access whenever the Court requires them. In a court where the presiding officer is in another district, a bundle whose custodian is not on the record cannot be produced when he asks for it, and the hearing is lost.

binds.target: document record - named custodian of the physical documents

requirements.how: Custody lies with the Superintendent or the Board Clerk, or as the Presiding Officer of the Court decides.
requirements.test: Every physically held document names a custodian drawn from the roles the rule permits; a query by case number returns the custodian, and a custody handover changes the name on the record.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 13.1 says physical documents shall be preserved in the custody of the Superintendent or Board Clerk, or as may be decided by the Presiding Officer of the Court, and rule 3.12 requires them to be maintained so as to ensure ready and prompt access whenever required by the Court. The rule fixes a determinate custodian and leaves the Presiding Officer free to name another; recording which of them holds a given bundle is the record of that allocation rather than an addition to it.
