requirements.statement: The system MUST require the accused to be present physically at the SARAS Court or at a Remote Point Location when the plea is recorded.
requirements.why: Rule 5.1 does not permit the plea to be taken from wherever the accused happens to be. A workflow that opens a video link to the accused's own phone and records a plea from it produces a plea the accused can disown, and in a cheque case the plea is the hinge on which a summary trial either concludes quickly or turns into a full contest.

binds.target: plea recording - place of the accused

requirements.test: Recording a plea requires the accused's location to be the SARAS Court or a notified Remote Point Location, or a place directed by the presiding officer with that direction recorded.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 5.1 says the accused shall remain present physically at the SARAS Court or at a Remote Point Location, or as directed by the Presiding Officer, and it stands at the head of the rule that governs recording of the plea. The two named places, and the Presiding Officer's power to direct another, are the sub-rule's own, so a plea taken from wherever the accused happens to be sitting is outside it.

requirements.statement: The system MUST capture the plea as a physically signed document, scanned and uploaded with a self-attested copy of an accepted proof of identity.
requirements.why: Rule 5.2 routes the plea through the physical-signature mode of rule 3.5. A plea recorded only as a screen entry by a clerk has no signature attributable to the accused; when he later resiles from it, there is nothing on the record to hold him to.

binds.target: plea recording - signature and identity proof

requirements.how: The signed plea is scanned with a self-attested copy of a driving licence, election card, passport, PAN card, Aadhaar card or other identity proof the court permits, and uploaded to the record.
requirements.test: A plea cannot be marked recorded without a scanned signed plea document and an identity proof attached.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 5.2 says a physical copy of the signed plea document shall be recorded in the manner provided in paragraph 3.5, and rule 3.5 requires the physically signed document, accompanied by a self-attested copy of a driving licence, election card, passport, PAN card, Aadhaar card or other identity proof the court permits, to be scanned and uploaded so as to form part of the judicial record. The signature and the identity proof are both conditions of the route the plea is sent down.

requirements.statement: The system MUST furnish the copies due to the accused in electronic form by one of the prescribed electronic modes.
requirements.why: Rule 5.3 makes electronic supply the ordinary course in a SARAS case. Where the court's workflow can only print and hand over, the accused in a remote-adjudication case, who may be answering from a video-enabled room in a district court hundreds of kilometres from Ahmedabad, has no way to receive his papers, and the trial cannot move past the supply stage.

binds.target: supply of copies to the accused - electronic modes

requirements.how: By electronic mail, by a recognised electronic messaging service, or on a digital storage device procured at the cost of the accused.
requirements.test: All three electronic modes are selectable when supplying copies, and the mode used with its date is recorded on the case.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 5.3 says copies of the complaint, documents, statements and other papers required to be supplied to the accused under law shall ordinarily be furnished in electronic form, and lists the three modes: electronic mail, a recognised electronic messaging service, or a digital storage device procured at the cost of the accused. The direction and the closed list of modes are both in the sub-rule.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record supply of the accused's copies to a person nominated by the accused, or to the pleader appearing for him, as valid compliance where the accused does not possess the facility to receive electronic copies.
requirements.why: Rule 5.4 is cast as a 'shall': where the accused does not possess the necessary facility, the electronic copies shall be furnished to his nominee or to his pleader, and such supply shall be deemed valid compliance with the statutory requirement. Without the nominee or pleader recorded as the recipient, the supply appears on the record as never made to the accused, and the defence can take the point at the plea stage and force a fresh supply.

binds.target: supply record - nominee or pleader as recipient

requirements.test: The supply record accepts a nominee or the pleader as the recipient with the relationship stated, and the supply is reported as compliant.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 5.4 says that where the accused does not possess the necessary facility to receive electronic copies, such copies shall be furnished to a person duly nominated by the accused or to the pleader appearing for him, and that such supply shall be deemed to be valid compliance of the statutory requirement. The deeming is what makes the alternative recipient a compliant one, and it is in the sub-rule's own words.

requirements.statement: The system MUST supply printed copies to the accused free of cost where he is unable to access or receive copies in electronic mode.
requirements.why: Rule 5.5 preserves the statutory mandate for the accused who has no electronic facility, and makes the free printed supply a direction of the presiding officer. A digital-only workflow silently excludes the individual drawer of a dishonoured cheque, who is often the least equipped party in the case, and the conviction that follows is open to attack for want of supply.

binds.target: supply of copies to the accused - free printed fallback

requirements.how: The printed copies are supplied free of cost as directed by the Presiding Officer of the Court.
requirements.test: Where the accused is recorded as unable to receive electronic copies, a free printed supply can be directed and fulfilled, with no charge raised against the accused.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 5.5 says that only where the accused is unable to access or does not possess the facility to receive copies in electronic mode, printed copies of the papers shall be supplied to him free of cost, in compliance with the statutory mandate, as directed by the Presiding Officer of the Court. The condition, the free supply and the person who directs it are all stated.

requirements.statement: The system MUST require a party filing a document during the hearing to furnish a copy to the opposite party forthwith.
requirements.why: Rules 4.22 and 4.23 place the duty on the filing party, ordinarily in electronic mode. In a remote hearing the opposite party cannot see what was handed up; without a served copy on the record the document is effectively filed behind his back, and any order made on it is vulnerable.

binds.target: in-hearing filing - supply to the opposite party

requirements.how: Supply is by electronic mail, a recognised electronic messaging service or another feasible electronic mode; where the opposite party cannot receive electronically, in physical form as the court directs.
requirements.test: A document filed during a hearing raises a supply task on the filing party that must be completed before the hearing is closed.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 4.22 says that where documents are filed by a party during the course of hearing, copies shall be furnished to the opposite party forthwith, ordinarily in electronic mode, by the party filing them; rule 4.23 names the electronic modes and the physical fallback where the opposite party cannot receive electronically. The duty, the person on whom it falls and the word forthwith are all in the sub-rules.

requirements.statement: The system MUST conduct video-conferencing hearings only on a High Court or Government approved platform with end-to-end encryption.
requirements.why: Both SARAS rule 4.21 and the 2025 rules require it. A SARAS hearing carries the accused's identity documents, the cheque and the bank's account particulars; conducted over a consumer meeting link it exposes all of that, and the unauthorised access the rules require to be reported becomes a routine risk.

binds.target: hearing platform - approved and encrypted

requirements.test: The hearing can be joined only through an approved platform held in configuration; an arbitrary meeting URL cannot be attached to a hearing.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 4.21 and rule 5(iv) of the 2025 rules use the same words: courts shall use only High Court or Government approved and secure video conferencing platforms equipped with end-to-end encryption to protect data and privacy. Approval and encryption are stated as conditions of the platform rather than as guidance about choosing one.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record the identity proof furnished to the court point coordinator by a person appearing through video conferencing, or the court's satisfaction dispensing with it.
requirements.why: Rule 6 is how the court knows who is on the screen. In a cheque case that means the accused answering summons and the bank witness proving the return memo. Without the identity proof or the recorded dispensation on the file, an accused can later say the person who appeared and pleaded was not him.

binds.target: appearance record - identity proof of a remote participant

requirements.how: The identity proof is one recognised by the Government of India or the State Government and is sent to the court point coordinator by electronic communication; where it is not readily available the court may allow participation on its own satisfaction.
requirements.test: Each remote appearance carries either an identity-proof reference or a recorded dispensation by the court.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 6 says the person appearing shall provide an identity proof as recognised by the Government of India or a State Government to the court point coordinator by electronic communication, and that where identity proof is not readily available the Court may, upon satisfaction, allow the person to participate without producing it. The rule creates exactly the two states the requirement holds, the proof and the dispensation on the court's satisfaction.

requirements.statement: The system MUST provide the accused an opportunity to consult his advocate before and after an examination conducted by video conferencing.
requirements.why: Rule 13(2) makes it the court's duty. In a remote cheque trial the accused and his advocate are often at different points, so unless the hearing schedule creates a private channel for them, the consultation simply does not happen and the accused is examined without advice, which is a ground of challenge that costs the complainant the judgment.

binds.target: remote examination - private consultation with the advocate

requirements.test: A remote examination of an accused offers a private consultation channel before and after the examination, and the fact that it was offered is recorded.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 13(2) says that where the person being examined is an accused, the court shall provide adequate opportunity to consult with his advocate before and after the video conferencing. The duty falls on the court, it is expressed as a shall, and both moments are named in the sub-rule.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT admit any person to a remote point during an examination other than the person being examined and those whose presence the coordinator deems administratively necessary.
requirements.why: Rule 13(5) puts the duty on the coordinator. Where the remote point is a room in a bank branch or a recovery office, the risk that a bank officer stands behind the witness is real, and a deposition taken with the complainant's employees present is worth nothing on appeal.

binds.target: remote point - persons admitted during an examination

requirements.test: The remote-point session records who was admitted, restricts joining to the person examined and the coordinator's listed necessary persons, and refuses others.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 13(5) says the coordinator at the designated place shall ensure that no person is present at the remote point, save and except the person being examined and those whose presence is deemed administratively necessary by the coordinator for the proceedings. The exclusion and its single exception are stated, and the requirement carries them without narrowing or widening either.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT permit recording or publication of proceedings conducted by video conferencing except where the court has expressly permitted it.
requirements.why: Rule 5(vii) and 5(viii) forbid unauthorised recording by any person at any point. A platform whose default toolbar offers a record button to every participant makes contempt trivially easy in a hearing where the accused's identity documents and the complainant's account particulars are on screen.

binds.target: hearing platform - recording and publication controls

requirements.test: Participant-side recording is disabled by default; enabling it requires a recorded court permission tied to the hearing.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 5(vii) says that unless expressly permitted by the Court, no person at the Court Point, the designated place, a Remote Point or an advocate's remote point shall record or publish the proceedings, and rule 5(viii) adds that there shall be no unauthorised recording by any person or entity. The prohibition, its reach to every point and the express-permission exception are all in the rules.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record a request by a party or witness for appearance through video conferencing in a criminal case.
requirements.why: Rule 11(1) puts the initiative on the party or the witness in a criminal case, save where the proceedings are initiated at the instance of the Court or on the request of the public prosecutor. With no request on the record, a remote appearance rests on nothing, and the accused's absence from the physical court looks like non-appearance, which in a cheque case leads to a warrant.

binds.target: appearance record - request for video conferencing

requirements.test: Every remote appearance in a criminal case carries either a request record naming its mover or a marker that the proceeding was initiated by the Court or on the public prosecutor's request; an appearance with neither cannot be listed.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 11(1) says that in criminal cases any party to the proceedings or a witness, save and except where proceedings are initiated at the instance of the Court or on the request of the public prosecutor, may move a request for presence and proceedings through video conferencing. The request is the route the rule prescribes for a criminal case, and the two situations in which none is needed are named, so recording it is the record of an express condition rather than an addition to one.

requirements.statement: The system MUST classify a criminal case instituted on a private complaint in Track I.
requirements.why: Schedule II Part B item 7 puts a criminal case on a private complaint, which is what a cheque case is, in Track I. The track drives the listing priority and the outer limit; a case sitting in the wrong track is scheduled against the wrong horizon, and in Gujarat's own scheme that is how a cheque case quietly becomes a three-year case.

authority.l: Case Flow Management Rules 2016, Sch.II Part B item 7

binds.target: case record - case flow track

requirements.how: The ministerial officer categorises the case and the judicial officer confirms the categorisation; the physical file takes the track colour, Track I being violet or indigo.
requirements.test: A case instituted on a private complaint is created in Track I, and the classification carries both the ministerial entry and the judicial confirmation.
requirements.statusReason: Schedule II Part B item 7 lists Criminal Case - Private Complaint against Track I, rule 21(A)(1) requires the presiding officer to classify criminal trials and proceedings according to the Schedule, and rule 3(i) and 3(ii) put the categorisation on the ministerial officer with confirmation by the judicial officer. The Track I entry is in the table itself. One blemish in the drafting is worth noting: rules 3(i) and 21(A)(1) both speak of Schedule-I, while the criminal table, and the entry this requirement uses, sit in Schedule II Part B.

requirements.statement: The system MUST compute and expose an outer date for concluding a criminal case on a private complaint at six months from institution.
requirements.why: Schedule II Part B item 7 prescribes six months as the outer limit for concluding a criminal case on a private complaint, the same horizon the NI Act sets for a summary cheque trial. Rule 3(iv) of the same rules gives Track I a maximum of nine months, and rule 21(A)(2) repeats nine months for Track I criminal cases, so the instrument divides against itself. A system that adopts the nine-month figure gives every cheque case three months of slack that the Schedule does not allow, and the monthly progress report will show the case as on time when it is already over.

authority.l: Case Flow Management Rules 2016, Sch.II Part B item 7

binds.target: case record - prescribed outer date for conclusion

requirements.test: A private-complaint criminal case shows an outer date six months from institution; the nine-month Track I figure is not used for this case type, and the divergence is surfaced rather than silently resolved.
requirements.statusReason: The instrument divides against itself and neither limb is a reading of ours. Schedule II Part B item 7 prescribes six months as the outer limit for concluding a criminal case on a private complaint. Rule 3(iv) gives Track I a maximum of nine months, and rule 21(A)(2) repeats nine months for Track I criminal trials, while the Schedule entry itself puts a private complaint in Track I. Nothing in the rules says which figure prevails where the specific entry and the track maximum disagree, so the requirement carries the shorter Schedule figure and surfaces the divergence rather than settling it by implementation.

requirements.statement: The system MUST require a written reason from the presiding judge before the track outer limit is extended or the case is moved to another track.
requirements.why: Rule 3(vi) allows the extension or shift only for valid reason recorded in writing. Without that constraint the outer date becomes an editable field, and the six-month horizon that gives a cheque case its priority is quietly reset by whoever holds the case.

binds.target: case record - amendment of the track or the outer date

requirements.test: The track and outer date cannot be changed without a reason text and a presiding-officer actor; the change and the reason appear on the case history.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 3(vi) says the Presiding Judge may, for valid reason to be recorded in writing, extend the time limit applicable to the concerned Track or shift a case from one Track to another. The writing, the reason and the person who may do it are all in the sub-rule. The only step outside the words cited is the civil-to-criminal carry that runs through rule 21(B), which this requirement does not itself cite.

requirements.statement: The system MUST produce a monthly report on the stage and progress of the cases scheduled to be listed in the next month, on the last working day of the third week of each month or five working days before the end of the business period, whichever is earlier.
requirements.why: Rule 3(vii) makes the report the mechanism by which the track scheme is actually enforced. Where the report has to be assembled by hand from a docket of several thousand cheque cases, it is not produced, and nothing else in the scheme notices a case running past its outer date.

binds.target: monthly case flow progress report

requirements.how: The report is prepared by the ministerial officer and placed before the court concerned.
requirements.test: The report generates on the prescribed date, covers the cases listed in the following month, and shows each case against its track and outer date.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 3(vii) says that on the last working day of the third week of every month, or five working days before the end of a particular business period, whichever is earlier, the Ministerial Officer shall cause a report about the stage and progress of the cases scheduled to be listed in the next month to be prepared, and shall place it before the Court concerned. The date, the content and both actors are in the sub-rule.

requirements.statement: The system SHOULD list a case for arguments within seven days of the completion of evidence.
requirements.why: Rule 9(13)(a) requires the case to be listed immediately after evidence is completed, and fixes seven days as the outer figure 'as far as possible' - it directs rather than commands, which is why this is a SHOULD; rule 21(B) carries the norm to a criminal trial. The gap between the close of evidence and arguments is where a cheque case with a six-month horizon loses months, because nothing triggers the listing.

binds.target: cause list - listing for arguments after evidence

requirements.test: Closing evidence on a case creates an arguments listing within seven days; a case with evidence closed and no arguments date inside seven days is reported as overdue.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 9(13)(a) says the case shall be listed immediately after the completion of evidence, for arguments, which shall as far as possible not be more than seven days. The seven days are qualified by as far as possible, which is why the level is SHOULD, and the sub-rule is written for a suit, reaching a criminal complaint only through rule 21(B). The softening and the carry together are why this is not firm.

requirements.statement: The system SHOULD record the magistrate's decision to try a case summarily before the trial commences.
requirements.why: Rule 102(1) says magistrates should consider the appropriateness and desirability of the summary procedure before commencing the trial, and rule 102(2) lists the cases in which it is not appropriate, including those prima facie likely to be long and complicated. The Manual directs the consideration; it does not in terms require the decision to be recorded, so both the level and the recording are a reading of the rule rather than its words. A system that infers summary trial from the offence alone leaves no trace that the discretion was exercised, and a defended cheque case that should have gone to summons procedure is tried summarily and has to be tried again.

binds.target: case record - decision to try summarily

requirements.test: The case carries a summary-trial decision with its date and actor, recorded before the first evidence event; the decision cannot be back-dated after evidence has begun.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 102(1) says that before commencing the trial of offences which can be tried summarily, magistrates should consider the appropriateness and desirability of following the summary procedure, and rule 102(2) lists the cases in which it is not appropriate, including those prima facie likely to be long and complicated; rule 101 sets out when the summary power exists at all. What the Manual directs is the consideration. It nowhere says the decision must be recorded, still less that it must be recorded before the trial begins, so both the recording and its timing are our reading.

requirements.statement: The system MUST raise the fixed bail bond fee when the accused is released on bond.
requirements.why: Schedule II Article 10 charges a fixed fee on a bail bond in a criminal case and on a recognizance for personal appearance. In a cheque case the accused who answers summons is released on a bond at his first appearance, so this fee attaches in every contested case; a system that does not raise it leaves a short-paid record that the office must reconcile case by case.

binds.target: fee ledger - bail bond fee at first appearance

requirements.how: Schedule II Article 10: two rupees on a bail-bond in a criminal case and on a recognizance to prosecute, to appear or otherwise.
requirements.test: Recording the accused's release on bond raises the Article 10 fee entry against the case.
requirements.statusReason: Schedule II Article 10 charges two rupees on a bail-bond in a criminal case and on a recognizance to prosecute, to appear or otherwise. The fee, its amount and the instruments it attaches to are all in the entry; what brings it into every contested cheque case is that the accused answering summons is released on such a bond, not any reading of the Article.

requirements.statement: The system MAY record an order apportioning or waiving the costs of video conferencing between the parties.
requirements.why: Rule 22 lets the court decide who bears the cost of the facility, of preparing and transmitting soft or certified copies to the remote coordinator, and of the translator, interpreter, special educator and remote coordinator, and lets it waive those costs. In a cheque case where the complainant is a bank and the accused an individual, an unrecorded cost order silently lands on whichever party the workflow bills by default.

binds.target: case record - order as to video conferencing costs

requirements.test: A video-conferencing cost order can be recorded against a party or waived, and the billing follows the order rather than a default.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 22 lets the Court determine and apportion the costs of video conferencing in a criminal case, naming the expenses of the facility, of preparing and transmitting soft or certified copies of the record to the coordinator at the remote point, and the fees payable to the translator, interpreter, special educator and coordinator; it says in terms that it shall be open to the Court to waive the costs. The power and the waiver are both stated, and the level is MAY because the rule is discretionary throughout.

requirements.statement: The system MUST store the schedule the court fixes when it allows a request for appearance through video conferencing.
requirements.why: Rule 11(3) lets the court fix the schedule for convening the video conferencing at the moment it allows the request. The rule states the court's power; that the schedule be held as data on the appearance rather than left in the prose of the order is the reading, not the text. Where it lives only in the order text, the hearing is listed off the ordinary board and the parties, the coordinator and the remote point are given different times, so the bank officer and the accused connect on different days.

binds.target: appearance record - schedule fixed for the video conferencing

requirements.test: An order allowing video conferencing captures the schedule as a dated, timed field on the appearance, and the hearing listing for that appearance is generated from it rather than entered separately.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 11(3) says that while allowing a request for video conferencing the Court may also fix the schedule for convening it. That is a power given to the court, and an order fixing the schedule in prose would satisfy the words. Requiring it to be held as a dated, timed field from which the listing is generated is the reading taken here, which is why the status is inferred.

requirements.statement: The system MUST set off the time spent in mediation, conciliation or Lok Adalat against the track time limit and extend the outer date proportionately.
requirements.why: Rule 9(2) requires the time to be set off and the track limit proportionately extended, and rule 21(B) carries the norm to the criminal side. A cheque case is the case most often sent to the Lok Adalat, since it is compoundable and the parties usually want money rather than a conviction. If the clock keeps running through the reference, a case that settles late but fails comes back already past its outer date and is treated as delayed when it was not.

binds.target: case record - outer date adjusted for time in alternative dispute resolution

requirements.test: Referring a case to mediation, conciliation or the Lok Adalat pauses the outer-date clock; on the failure report the outer date is extended by the elapsed period and the adjustment is visible on the case.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 9(2) says that where the report about failure of conciliation or mediation is received and the record returned, the time spent in the process shall be set off and the time limit under the respective Tracks shall proportionately stand extended. The set-off and the extension are both express. The sub-rule is drawn for a suit and names conciliation and mediation; extending it to a Lok Adalat reference in a criminal complaint runs through rule 21(B), and that carry is the inference.

requirements.statement: The system SHOULD relist a case within three days of the report that the alternative dispute resolution process has failed.
requirements.why: Rule 9(1) requires the matter to be listed within three days of the report, and rule 9(3) warns courts not to let the forum be used to prolong the case. The rule is written in civil terms, so its application to a criminal complaint runs through rule 21(B). Without the relisting trigger, a failed Lok Adalat reference leaves a cheque case dormant in the record room while its outer date runs.

binds.target: cause list - relisting after a failed settlement reference

requirements.test: Recording a failure report creates a listing within three days, and a case with a failure report and no listing inside three days is reported.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 9(1) says that on the filing of the report by the mediator, the conciliator or the Lok Adalat about the failure of the process, the suit shall be listed within three days after the report, and rule 9(3) warns courts not to allow the ADR forum to be abused to prolong the case. The three days are express, but the sub-rule lists the suit for framing of issues, a stage a criminal complaint does not have, so its application here runs through rule 21(B) with the corresponding changes. That transposition is the reading, and it is why the level is SHOULD and the status is not firm.

requirements.statement: The system MUST require the accused to be personally present at the SARAS Court when judgment is pronounced.
requirements.why: Rule 10.1 makes personal presence at pronouncement a distinct requirement from presence at the plea. A remote-adjudication workflow that treats pronouncement as one more video hearing will pronounce a conviction on a cheque case with the accused on a screen in another district, and the conviction warrant that follows cannot be executed against a person who was never before the court.

binds.target: judgment pronouncement - presence of the accused

requirements.how: The accused remains personally present at the SARAS Court at the time of pronouncement, or as and when the Presiding Officer directs.
requirements.test: A judgment cannot be marked pronounced unless the accused's presence at the SARAS Court is recorded, or a direction of the presiding officer to the contrary is on the record.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 10.1 says accused persons shall remain personally present at the SARAS Court at the time of pronouncement of judgment, or as and when directed by the Presiding Officer of the Court. Personal presence at pronouncement is stated as a requirement separate from the presence at the plea that rule 5.1 governs, and the only relaxation is a direction of the Presiding Officer.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT make e-payment the only mode by which a fine, penalty or compensation can be paid.
requirements.why: Rule 12 permits e-payment once the facility is enabled for the court, and until then payment by cash or another permissible mode. Compensation is the relief a cheque complainant actually came for. In a court where the facility is not yet live, a payment screen that offers only the electronic route leaves the accused unable to pay, the complainant unpaid, and the case unable to close.

binds.target: payment of fine and compensation - available modes

requirements.test: Where e-payment is not enabled for the court, cash and other permissible modes remain selectable, and the mode used is recorded against the payment.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 12.1 permits payment of fine, penalty or compensation through the e-payment facility once enabled for the Court, and rule 12.2 says that until such enablement, payment may be accepted by cash or such other permissible mode. Read together they make the electronic route conditional on enablement and keep cash open until it arrives, so an electronic-only payment screen would close a court where the facility is not yet live.

requirements.statement: The system MUST route the issue and execution of a conviction warrant through the ordinary procedure established by law rather than through the remote-adjudication workflow.
requirements.why: Rule 10.2 is the point at which a remote cheque case returns to the physical world. A warrant generated and treated as served inside the electronic workflow commits a person to prison on a record that no physical authority has acted on, which is the one step in a cheque case where the electronic record cannot stand alone.

binds.target: conviction warrant - issue, execution and compliance

requirements.test: A conviction warrant is produced as a signed instrument for execution through the ordinary process channel, and its execution is recorded from a physical return rather than closed inside the portal.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 10.2 says that in all cases where a person is produced before the Court pursuant to execution of a warrant, or where a person is required to be committed to prison upon issuance of a conviction warrant, the issuance, execution and compliance of such process shall be governed strictly by the procedure established by law. The word strictly, in a set of rules that otherwise makes the electronic record authoritative, is what puts this step outside the portal.

requirements.statement: The system MUST treat the electronic record maintained on the designated portal as the primary and authoritative judicial record of a SARAS case.
requirements.why: Rule 3.1 is the doctrinal core of the SARAS regime. Where a system keeps a parallel physical file as the authoritative one and the portal as a copy, the two diverge, and a cheque case is decided on whichever version the officer happens to be holding. The whole design of remote adjudication, in which the officer is never in the same building as the paper, depends on this being settled the other way.

binds.target: case record - the portal record as the authoritative record

requirements.test: Every document, order and rojnama entry of a SARAS case exists on the portal record, and no case artifact exists only outside it.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 3.1 says the electronic record maintained on the designated portal shall constitute the primary and authoritative judicial record; rule 3.2 requires complaints, affidavits, applications, evidence, orders, judgments and rojnama entries ordinarily to be accessed and acted upon in electronic form; and rule 4.10 makes the scanned electronic document the record of the Court notwithstanding that the physical original stays with the person producing it. The primacy is declared in terms and is not derived from the design of the establishment.

requirements.statement: The system MUST authenticate a document required to be signed by a token-based Digital Signature Certificate where the signatory holds one.
requirements.why: Rules 3.3, 3.4 and 4.19 require authentication that ensures verifiability, integrity and attribution, and discourage physical signing where a token or Aadhaar e-sign is available. A bank filing in bulk holds tokens for its authorised signatories; letting those filings through on a scanned wet signature loses the attribution that makes the electronic record authoritative in the first place.

binds.target: document authentication - token-based digital signature

requirements.test: A signatory with a registered token is offered only the token route, and a document signed with it records the certificate details on the record.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 3.3 requires documents that must be signed to be authenticated in a manner ensuring verifiability, integrity and attribution, and rule 3.4 gives exactly two modes: a token-based Digital Signature Certificate, or a physical signature where the person does not possess a token based digital signature. That condition is the gate, since the physical route opens only in the absence of a token. Rule 4.19 points the same way in softer words, saying physical signing shall ordinarily be discouraged where a token or Aadhaar e-sign is held, and clause 7.1 of the SOP makes the print-and-sign route the fallback for a person with no digital signature.

requirements.statement: The system MUST capture, where authentication is by physical signature, the scanned signed document together with a self-attested copy of an accepted proof of identity.
requirements.why: Rule 3.5 is the fallback for a person without a token. An individual accused, and the small payee who files without an advocate, will always use it. If the identity proof is not captured with the signed page, the signature on the record is attributable to nobody, and the document fails the verifiability that rule 3.3 requires.

binds.target: document authentication - physical signature route

requirements.how: The person physically signs, and the signed document accompanied by a self-attested copy of a driving licence, election card, passport, PAN card, Aadhaar card or other identity proof the court permits is scanned and uploaded to form part of the judicial record.
requirements.test: A physically signed upload cannot be completed without an identity proof attached, and both pages land on the same document record.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 3.5 says that where authentication is required by physical signature, the person shall physically sign, and the signed document accompanied by a self-attested copy of one of the listed proofs of identity shall be scanned and uploaded so as to form part of the judicial record; rule 3.6 then deems what is done that way duly authenticated. The identity proof is part of what the rule requires to be uploaded, not an addition made to it.

requirements.statement: The system MUST require the Presiding Officer to digitally sign a document scanned at the Remote Adjudication Point before it forms part of the official record.
requirements.why: Rule 3.7 makes the officer's digital signature the act that admits a scanned document to the record, after the ministerial staff have scanned, OCR-enabled, checked and verified it. Without that step, anything a clerk uploads is on the file, and in a court where the officer is in another district there is no other moment at which he sees what has been added.

binds.target: document intake - presiding officer's digital signature on scanned documents

requirements.how: The ministerial staff of the Remote Adjudication Point scan, OCR-enable, check and verify the document per the High Court's scanning and digitisation SOP, and send it to the SARAS Court, where the Presiding Officer digitally signs it.
requirements.test: A scanned document sits in a pending state until the presiding officer signs it; only then does it appear as part of the official record.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 3.7 says that once documents scanned, OCR-enabled, checked and verified by the ministerial staff of the Remote Adjudication Point are received by the SARAS Court, the Presiding Officer shall digitally sign them, and that they shall then be deemed to form part of the official record of the Court; rule 4.15 says the same for documents authenticated on the portal. The signature is the act that admits the document, and the sequence is the rule's own.

requirements.statement: The system MUST assign exhibit numbers to the documents of a SARAS case in conformity with rule 76 of the Criminal Manual.
requirements.why: SARAS rule 4.13 sends exhibit and bookmark assignment straight back to Criminal Manual rule 76, under which each document bears an exhibit number and a serial number as it comes before the court. An independent numbering scheme invented by the portal produces a record whose exhibit numbers do not match the Roznama, the deposition or the judgment, and a certified copy taken from it is unusable on appeal.

binds.target: exhibit assignment - conformity with Criminal Manual rule 76

requirements.how: The designated staff member assigns bookmarks, exhibits or marks promptly and correctly according to the nature of the document; each document bears an exhibit number and a serial number as it comes before the court.
requirements.test: Exhibit numbers run in the order documents come before the court, and the exhibit list on the rojnama matches the exhibit numbers on the documents themselves.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 4.13 says the designated staff member shall promptly and correctly assign bookmarks, exhibits or marks strictly in accordance with the nature of the documents and in conformity with rule 76 of the Criminal Manual, and rule 76 requires each document to bear an exhibit number and a serial number as it comes before the Court. The conformity is directed by name, so an independent numbering scheme is not a permitted variant.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record the rojnama in the Case Information System at the conclusion of proceedings on each date of hearing and place it for the Presiding Officer's digital authentication.
requirements.why: Rule 4.20 fixes both the moment and the authentication. A rojnama written up days later from memory, or never authenticated, is not the faithful history of the case that Criminal Manual rule 76 requires; and in a remote court the rojnama is the only account of what happened, since no party and no officer shares a room.

binds.target: rojnama entry for a date of hearing

requirements.how: The designated staff member records the rojnama in the Case Information System under the Case Proceedings or Business block; it is then placed for the Presiding Officer's digital signature and on signature forms part of the official record.
requirements.test: Closing a hearing creates a rojnama entry dated that day, which cannot become part of the record until digitally signed by the presiding officer.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 4.20 says that at the conclusion of proceedings on each date of hearing the designated staff member shall accurately record the rojnama in the Case Information System under the Case Proceedings or Business block, that it shall thereafter be placed for digital authentication by the Presiding Officer, and that upon that signature it forms part of the official record. Rule 76 supplies what the rojnama is for, a faithful history of the case kept from day to day. The moment and the authentication are both in the sub-rule.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT record ministerial acts such as the receipt of process fees or the preparation of summonses in the Roznama.
requirements.why: Rule 76 excludes them expressly and requires the Roznama to be as concise as possible while remaining a faithful history. A system that writes every event of its own audit log into the rojnama buries the judicial history of a cheque case under fee receipts and process-generation entries, and the officer reading the file cannot see what was actually done in court.

binds.target: rojnama content - exclusion of ministerial events

requirements.test: Fee receipts, process generation and similar ministerial events appear in the audit trail but not in the rojnama; the rojnama for a typical cheque hearing is a handful of lines.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 76 says the Roznama is not to include a record of ministerial acts, such as receipt of bhatta or process fees, the preparation of summonses and the like, and requires it to be as concise as possible while remaining a faithful history of the case. The exclusion is stated and it names the very classes of event the requirement keeps out.

requirements.statement: The system MUST sub-number an order on an interlocutory application, or a document filed in continuation of an existing exhibit, below the parent exhibit rather than assigning it an independent exhibit number.
requirements.why: Rule 4.17 gives the example: an order below Exhibit-5 is Exhibit-5/1. Assigning a fresh number breaks the link between the application and the order on it, and in a cheque case with a long series of applications for exemption from personal appearance the record becomes impossible to follow at the appellate stage.

binds.target: exhibit numbering - sub-numbering below a parent exhibit

requirements.how: An order passed below Exhibit-5 is marked Exhibit-5/1 and is not assigned an independent exhibit number.
requirements.test: An order recorded against an application exhibited as 5 is numbered 5/1, and the next independent document takes the next whole number.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 4.17 says that where an order is passed upon an interlocutory application, or a document is filed in continuation of an existing exhibit, it shall be sub-numbered or itemised below the original exhibit, and gives the worked example that an order passed below Exhibit-5 shall be marked Exhibit-5/1 and shall not be assigned an independent exhibit number. The rule and its example are both in the text.

requirements.statement: The system MUST generate orders, judgments and depositions directly in PDF rather than by printing, signing and scanning them.
requirements.why: Rule 4.18 requires direct generation, not a print-sign-scan cycle. A scanned judgment has no text layer, cannot be searched, quoted or indexed, and is a poor thing to send to an appellate court that receives the record electronically under rule 14.

binds.target: orders, judgments and depositions as natively generated signed PDFs

requirements.test: A judgment, an order and a deposition produced by the system are each PDFs with a selectable text layer, and no page in them is a scanned image.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 4.18 says all orders, judgments and depositions shall be directly generated in PDF format. Directly generated is what excludes the print, sign and scan cycle, so the requirement carries the sub-rule's own word rather than reasoning from the value of a text layer.

requirements.statement: The system MUST require an order sheet typed by a stenographer to be digitally signed by the magistrate before it is uploaded to the Case Information System.
requirements.why: Rule 8.1 allows magistrates to dictate order sheets to stenographers online during or after the hearing, and requires the signature before upload. An unsigned order sheet on the CIS is indistinguishable from a signed one to anyone reading the case, and in a remote court where nobody sees the officer sign, that is how an undictated or altered order enters the record.

binds.target: order sheet - signature before upload

requirements.test: An order sheet cannot be uploaded to the CIS in an unsigned state; the upload action requires the signature in the same step.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 8.1 says magistrates can dictate the order sheets to stenographers online during or after hearing, and that the typed order sheets shall be digitally signed by the magistrates before uploading them on CIS. The signature and its position ahead of the upload are both in that sentence.

requirements.statement: The system MUST make a registered matter available first in the Presiding Officer's account and only after his verification route it to the designated court staff.
requirements.why: Rule 4.12 fixes the order. If a newly registered cheque case goes straight to ministerial processing, the exhibits and bookmarks are assigned before the officer has seen the matter at all, and the first judicial look at the file happens after the record has already been shaped.

binds.target: case routing after registration - presiding officer before court staff

requirements.test: A newly registered matter appears only in the presiding officer's queue; the staff queue receives it after his verification is recorded.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 4.12 says that upon registration the matter shall first be made available for perusal in the user account of the Presiding Officer on the designated portal, and that upon verification by him it shall thereafter proceed to the user account of the designated Court staff for further ministerial processing. The order is the sub-rule's own, expressed as first and thereafter.

requirements.statement: The system MUST govern the maintenance, classification, retention and destruction of the electronic record on the designated portal by rules 361 to 367 of the Criminal Manual.
requirements.why: Rule 7.1 applies the 1977 record rules to the electronic record so far as they can apply. A digital archive run on a storage-management policy of its own will destroy or migrate the record of a cheque case on a schedule the court never adopted, and the classification the Criminal Manual requires will not exist to argue about.

binds.target: electronic record - retention policy derived from the Criminal Manual

requirements.test: Every electronic case record carries a Criminal Manual classification and the retention period that attaches to it, and no destruction runs outside that policy.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 7.1 says the maintenance, classification, retention and destruction of electronic records maintained on the designated portal shall be governed by, and carried out in conformity with, rules 361 to 367 of the Criminal Manual, insofar as they are applicable to electronic records. The application of the 1977 record rules to the electronic record is directed by name and by range.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT despatch the record of a substantive criminal proceeding to the record room until the period for appeal or revision has expired, or where an appeal or revision has been instituted, until it is disposed of.
requirements.why: Rule 361 sets the condition and adds, as a precaution, that records be kept intact in the sequence of institution serial numbers for two months beyond that period before filing orders are taken. A cheque case record archived on judgment cannot be produced when the appellate court calls for it under SARAS rule 14, and the appeal stalls on the record's absence.

binds.target: record room - despatch precondition

requirements.test: The despatch action is unavailable while the appeal or revision period is running or an appeal or revision is pending, and the two-month precautionary hold is applied before filing orders are sought.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 361 says the record of a substantive criminal proceeding should not be considered due for despatch to the record room until the expiry of the period of appeal or revision application and, if one has been instituted, until after its disposal, and adds as a matter of precaution that records be kept intact in the sequence of institution serial numbers for two months beyond that period before filing orders are put up. The condition and the precautionary hold are both stated, though the Manual expresses them as should rather than shall, which the requirement's MUST NOT tightens.

requirements.statement: The system MUST classify every paper on the record into file A, B, C or D immediately after the filing order is passed.
requirements.why: Rule 362 requires the arrangement into four files, and rule 363 attaches the retention period to the class. Without the classification recorded per document, the retention period cannot be applied at all, and either everything is kept for ever or the retention run picks a single period for the whole case.

binds.target: document record - Criminal Manual file classification

requirements.how: Papers to be preserved permanently go to file A; semi-permanent papers such as judgments of a court other than the Sessions Court to file B; papers bearing on the merits such as depositions and documents produced in evidence not to be returned to the parties to file C; papers with no bearing on the merits such as vakalatnamas and remand orders to file D.
requirements.test: Passing the filing order requires each document to carry an A, B, C or D classification, and an unclassified document blocks the filing order.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 362(i) says that immediately after the passing of the filing order in any case the record shall be arranged in four files marked A, B, C and D, and rule 363 defines what belongs in each and attaches a different retention period to each. The classification, its timing and its four values are all in the rules.

requirements.statement: The system MUST compute the destruction date of a paper from the class it was given, running from the final decision of the case in the trial court where no appeal or revision was filed and from the final decision of the appellate or revisional court where one was.
requirements.why: Rule 363 fixes the periods and the starting point. A retention engine that runs from the date the document was created will destroy a deposition in a cheque case five years after it was recorded rather than five years after the case ended, which in a contested case can be while the appeal is still pending.

binds.target: document record - destruction date by class

requirements.how: File A permanently; file B destroyed after thirty years; file C after five years; file D after six months. The period is computed from the date of the final decision of the case in the trial court where no appeal or revision application has been filed, and from the date of the final decision of the appellate or revisional court where one has been filed.
requirements.test: The destruction date on a document equals its class period added to the case's final-decision date - the appellate or revisional decision date where an appeal or revision was filed - and never to the document's own date.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 363(5) fixes the periods, permanent for file A, thirty years for file B, five years for file C and six months for file D, and rule 363(6) fixes the starting point: the period is computed from the date of the final decision of the case in the trial Court where no appeal or revision application has been filed, and from the date of the final decision of the appellate or revisional Court where one has. Both the periods and the event they run from are in the rule.

requirements.statement: The system MUST apply the longer of the two retention periods prescribed for a signed vakalatnama.
requirements.why: The sources divide. Criminal Manual rule 363 puts vakalatnamas in file D, destroyed after six months. Clause 10.2 of the Gujarat e-Filing SOP requires the signed vakalatnama to be preserved for at least two years after final disposal, including disposal by the superior appellate court, and SARAS rule 13.2 adopts that clause for retention of originals in a SARAS case. A system that follows the Criminal Manual alone destroys the very document whose authenticity the SOP anticipates being questioned, while the appeal in the cheque case is still running.

binds.target: retention policy - vakalatnama

requirements.test: A signed vakalatnama in a SARAS case is retained until at least two years after final appellate disposal, and the six-month file D period does not trigger its destruction.
requirements.statusReason: The two instruments give different answers for the same document and neither yields to the other. Rule 363 puts vakalatnamas in file D, to be destroyed after six months. Clause 10.2 of the e-Filing SOP requires the signed vakalatnama to be preserved at least two years after final disposal, including disposal by the superior appellate court, and SARAS rule 13.2 adopts clause 10 for retention of originals in a SARAS case, while SARAS rule 7.1 sends the electronic record back to rules 361 to 367 of the Manual. The rules therefore point at each other, and nothing in either says which prevails, so the requirement takes the longer period rather than deciding the conflict by implementation.

requirements.statement: The system MUST preserve the register of cases before Judicial Magistrates and Metropolitan Magistrates for thirty years from the expiry of the last year in the volume.
requirements.why: Rule 364 sets the period for the registers, as distinct from the case papers. In a court hearing cheque cases in bulk the register is the only index by which an old case can be found once the papers have gone to the record room, and a register purged with the case files leaves the record unsearchable.

binds.target: register retention - registers of cases before magistrates

requirements.test: The case register carries a thirty-year retention computed from the expiry of the last year in the volume, independent of the retention on the case papers it indexes.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 364, under the heading for papers not forming part of court proceedings, says the Register of Cases before Judicial Magistrates and Metropolitan Magistrates shall be preserved for thirty years from the expiry of the last year of the Register in the same volume of Registers. The period, the register and the starting point are all named in the rule.

requirements.statement: The system MUST restrict access to the pleadings and documents filed electronically in a case to the advocates for the parties and to the party-in-person.
requirements.why: Clause 11.1 confines access to them. A SARAS cheque case file holds the accused's identity documents and the complainant's account particulars for thousands of borrowers; a portal that lets any logged-in advocate open any case turns the docket into a source of personal data at scale.

binds.target: case file access - parties' advocates and the party-in-person

requirements.test: An advocate not on record for a party cannot open the pleadings or documents of that case; the attempt is refused and logged.
requirements.statusReason: Clause 11.1 says access to the pleadings and the documents filed electronically in an Action will be provided only to the advocates for the parties or to the concerned party-in-person. The word only is what makes this a restriction rather than a description of who ordinarily looks at a file.

requirements.statement: The system MUST store e-filings on a server under the control and directions of the court, with each filing separately labelled and encrypted.
requirements.why: Clause 17 requires it. An institutional filer's cheque bundles carry account numbers, addresses and signatures; held on a shared or vendor-controlled store, or unencrypted, they are outside the court's control while remaining the primary judicial record under SARAS rule 3.1.

binds.target: storage - court-controlled, labelled and encrypted e-filing store

requirements.test: Filings are held encrypted at rest on court-controlled infrastructure, each with its own label, and access is only through the court's own access-control path.
requirements.statusReason: Clause 17 says e-filings will be stored on an exclusive server maintained under the control and directions of the Court, that each filing will be separately labelled and encrypted to facilitate identification and retrieval, and that access will be restricted in the manner provided. Court control, the label and the encryption are each stated in the clause.

requirements.statement: The system SHOULD maintain a mirror image of the e-filings on servers at a different geographical location for continuity of operations.
requirements.why: Clause 17 provides that a mirror image of the e-filings may be maintained on servers at different geographical locations for continuity of operations in case of disaster, natural calamity or breakdown. The clause is permissive on its face; treating the mirror as something a system ought to have is a reading of it in the light of SARAS rule 3.1, which makes the electronic record the primary and authoritative judicial record. On that footing the loss of the store is the loss of the case, and a court trying tens of thousands of cheque cases has no paper file to fall back on.

binds.target: storage - geographically separate mirror

requirements.test: A restore from the mirror reproduces the portal record of a sample case in full, including its digital signatures.
requirements.statusReason: The last sentence of clause 17 says that for continuity of operations in case of disaster, natural calamity or breakdown, a mirror image of the e-filings available on the servers located in the Court may be maintained at different geographical locations, as decided from time to time by the Court. The clause is permissive on its face and leaves the decision with the Court. Treating the mirror as something a system ought to have is a reading of it against SARAS rule 3.1, which makes the electronic record the primary and authoritative judicial record and so makes the loss of the store the loss of the case.

requirements.statement: The system MUST generate a hash value for an audio or video file included in an e-filing.
requirements.why: Clause 8.4 puts that duty on the Administrator. Where a cheque case turns on a recorded conversation or a video of a handover, a file on the record with no hash cannot be shown to be the file that was filed, and its integrity is open to challenge at the very point it matters.

binds.target: document record - hash value of an audio or video filing

requirements.test: An audio or video upload records a hash value against the document; recomputing the hash on the stored file reproduces it.
requirements.statusReason: Clause 8.4 says that where on-line e-filing includes audio or video files, the Administrator shall generate a hash value. The duty and the class of file it attaches to are both in the clause.

requirements.statement: The system MUST have every order, judgment and deposition digitally signed by the Presiding Officer through the designated portal.
requirements.why: Rule 4.18 puts the signature on the same footing as the generation. An unsigned judgment sitting on the portal is indistinguishable from a signed one to anyone reading the case, and in a court where nobody is in the room when the officer signs, an image of a signature is not a verifiable one when the appellate court receives the record electronically under rule 14.

binds.target: orders, judgments and depositions - presiding officer's digital signature

requirements.test: A judgment carries a verifiable digital signature of the presiding officer applied on the portal; a judgment without one cannot be released to the parties or transmitted on appeal.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 4.18 requires all orders, judgments and depositions to be digitally signed by the Presiding Officer through a designated portal, in the same sentence that requires them to be generated in PDF. The signature is not a practice built on top of the sub-rule; it is half of what the sub-rule directs.

requirements.statement: The system MUST treat a digitally signed electronic copy generated from the record on the designated portal as a certified copy for all legal purposes.
requirements.why: Rule 11.2 says so expressly. Where the system offers only a printed and manually attested copy, a party in a SARAS cheque case has to travel to Ahmedabad for the judgment he needs to file an appeal, in a case that was tried entirely at a distance, and the appeal period runs while he does.

binds.target: certified copy generated from the digitally signed electronic record

requirements.how: Issuance is governed by Chapter XXII of the Criminal Manual; copies are generated from the digitally signed electronic record on the designated portal.
requirements.test: A certified copy of a judgment can be obtained as a digitally signed electronic file, and it is accepted as a certified copy without a further physical attestation.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 11.2 says certified copies shall ordinarily be generated from the digitally signed electronic record available on the designated portal, and that such digitally signed electronic copies shall be treated as certified copies for all legal purposes; rule 11.1 keeps issuance governed by Chapter XXII of the Criminal Manual. The equivalence the requirement rests on is stated in the sub-rule in those words.

requirements.statement: The system MUST carry on a certified copy of a digitally converted document a statement that the copy is generated from the digitally converted document filed in court.
requirements.why: Rule 11.3 requires the statement. Without it a certified copy of a scanned cheque looks like a certified copy of the instrument itself, and a party relying on it in another proceeding, a civil suit on the same cheque for instance, misrepresents what the court actually holds.

binds.target: certified copy - provenance statement

requirements.test: A certified copy of a scanned document carries the statement on its face; a certified copy of a natively electronic order does not.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 11.3 says that when certified copies of digitally converted documents are issued, they shall contain a statement that the copy is generated from the digitally converted document filed in court. Both the trigger and the substance of the statement are in the sub-rule.

requirements.statement: The system MUST supply a certified copy through the medium the applicant specified in the application.
requirements.why: Rule 11.4 makes the medium the applicant's choice, subject only to the device not being obsolete. A workflow that always emails will fail the applicant who needs the copy on a storage device because the record is too large for mail, and one that always uses a device makes an applicant in another district travel to collect it.

binds.target: certified copy application - medium of supply

requirements.how: The medium is electronic mail, a recognised electronic messaging service, or a digital storage device that has not become obsolete.
requirements.test: The application captures the medium; the supply record shows the copy went out by that medium.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 11.4 says the applicant shall specify in the application the medium through which certified copies are sought, naming electronic mail, a recognised electronic messaging service or a digital storage device that has not become obsolete, and that certified copies shall be supplied through the medium specified in the application. The applicant's choice and the court's obligation to follow it are both stated.

requirements.statement: The system MUST compute the charge for a certified copy supplied by electronic means on the prescribed per-megabyte scale.
requirements.why: Rule 11.5 fixes a minimum of fifty rupees for up to twenty-five megabytes and fifty rupees for each further twenty-five megabytes, with the cost of the storage device borne by the applicant in addition. A cheque case record with scanned bank statements runs to hundreds of megabytes, so a system charging a single flat copying fee will under-recover on every large record and cannot reconcile its copy account.

binds.target: certified copy - charge computation

requirements.how: A minimum of fifty rupees for up to twenty-five megabytes as handling charges, and fifty rupees for each additional twenty-five megabytes; where supply is on a digital storage device, the actual cost of the device is borne by the applicant in addition.
requirements.test: A copy of sixty megabytes is charged for three blocks; supply on a device adds the device cost as a separate line.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 11.5 sets the scale in a table: a minimum of fifty rupees for up to twenty-five megabytes as handling charges, and thereafter fifty rupees for each additional twenty-five megabytes, with the actual cost of the electronic device borne by the applicant in addition where supply is on one. The figures and the block size are the sub-rule's own.

requirements.statement: The system MUST produce, with a certified copy supplied in electronic form, a digitally signed endorsement page stating the date of the application, the date it was granted and the date the copy was ready for delivery.
requirements.why: Rule 11.7 prescribes the endorsement, and it is what the appellate court uses to exclude the copying time from the limitation for the appeal. Without those three dates on the copy, a convicted drawer in a cheque case cannot show why his appeal was filed when it was.

binds.target: certified copy - endorsement page

requirements.how: The endorsement is made on a separate page by the concerned ministerial staff and is digitally signed by the staff member supplying the copy; compliance with the Criminal Manual is ensured through digital endorsements and digital signatures.
requirements.test: Every electronically supplied certified copy carries an endorsement page with the three dates and a verifiable staff signature.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 11.7 says that at the time of supplying certified copies in electronic form the concerned ministerial staff shall make an endorsement on a separate page indicating the date on which the application was made, the date on which it was granted and the date on which the copy was ready for delivery, and that the endorsement shall be digitally signed by the staff member supplying the copies; rule 11.6 requires compliance with the Criminal Manual to be secured through digital endorsements and signatures. The separate page, the three dates and the signature are all directed.

requirements.statement: The system MUST furnish a certified copy within ten days of a complete application.
requirements.why: Rule 384 sets the period, running from the day the application is presented where it is complete, and from the date it is granted in other cases. In a cheque case the copy of the judgment is the document an appeal cannot be filed without, so a copy queue with no service clock silently eats into the appeal period.

binds.target: certified copy queue - ten day service clock

requirements.how: The ten days run from the day on which the application is presented where the application is complete, and in other cases from the date on which the application is granted.
requirements.test: A complete copy application carries a due date ten days out, and the queue reports applications past it.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 384 says copies shall be furnished within ten days of the application, computed from the day on which it is presented where the application is complete, and in other cases from the date on which the application is granted. The period and both starting points are in the rule.

requirements.statement: The system MUST endorse the cause of delay on a certified copy furnished after the ten day period.
requirements.why: Rule 384 requires the cause of delay to be endorsed on the copy where further delay is unavoidable. That endorsement is the applicant's evidence when the appellate court asks why the appeal is late; a copy delivered late with nothing on its face leaves him unable to explain the gap.

binds.target: certified copy - endorsement of the cause of delay

requirements.test: A copy delivered after the due date cannot be issued without a cause-of-delay text, and the text appears on the copy.
requirements.statusReason: The same sentence of rule 384 makes the ten days subject to further delay being unavoidable, and says that in that case the cause of delay shall be endorsed on the copy. The endorsement and the document it goes on are both stated.

requirements.statement: The system MUST estimate the cost of a certified copy, including postage where the copy is to be sent by post, before the copying work is undertaken.
requirements.why: Rules 380 and 381 require the estimate first and the deposit of the estimated cost before the work is taken on hand. Copying begun before the estimate produces work nobody has paid for, and in a busy magistrate's copy section that is how a copy application sits for weeks with the file already extracted from the record room.

binds.target: certified copy - cost estimate before copying

requirements.how: The estimate covers all probable costs of the copies including postage where they are to be sent by post; an applicant not entitled to a free copy is called on to deposit the estimated cost and make up any other deficiency.
requirements.test: The copy workflow produces an estimate and takes a deposit before the copying task can be started.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 380 says the office shall estimate the costs of the copies before the copying work is undertaken, and that the estimate should as far as possible cover all probable costs including postage where the copies are to be sent by post. Rule 381 then requires an applicant not entitled to a free copy to deposit the estimated cost and make up any other deficiency before the copying work is taken on hand. The order of the steps is what the two rules fix.

requirements.statement: The system MUST raise a search fee where the description of the document in a copy application is incorrect or deficient and the record has to be searched to find it.
requirements.why: Rule 382 makes the fee payable per year of records searched, whether or not the document is found and whether or not the copy is granted. In a court with tens of thousands of cheque cases a search across years is real work. Note that the rate in rule 382, one rupee for each year searched, is the 1977 figure taken from an OCR of the first edition of the Manual, and the current rate must be verified against the official text and the fee tables in force.

binds.target: certified copy application - search fee

requirements.test: A copy application marked as requiring a search raises a fee computed per year searched, at a rate held as data rather than hard-coded.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 382 says that where the description of the documents given in the application is incorrect or deficient and a search of the records is in consequence necessary, a fee shall be payable for each year of which the records are searched, whether the document is found or not and whether the copy is granted or not. The trigger, the unit of charge and both indifferences are in the rule. Its rate, one rupee for each year, is the 1977 figure taken from an OCR of the first edition of the Manual, which is why the requirement holds the rate as data rather than fixing it.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT refuse a certified copy to a person who is a stranger to the case where the application is made in accordance with the rules for the grant of certified copies.
requirements.why: Clause 11.3 of the SOP preserves the stranger's entitlement alongside the access restriction in clause 11.1. A system that implements the access restriction as a blanket rule will also block the certified-copy route, and a guarantor or a subsequent endorsee of the same cheque, who has no access to the file but a real interest in the judgment, cannot obtain it at all.

binds.target: certified copy application - applicant who is a stranger to the case

requirements.test: A user with no association to the case can lodge a certified-copy application and receive the copy on the ordinary terms, while remaining unable to browse the case file.
requirements.statusReason: Clause 11.3 says a stranger to the Action is entitled to obtain the certified copy of the pleadings and documents filed in the Action in accordance with the relevant rules, and clause 11.2 gives the parties' advocates and the party-in-person the same entitlement. The stranger's right is stated in the SOP alongside the access restriction in clause 11.1, so the two are meant to stand together and a blanket implementation of the restriction would defeat an express entitlement.

requirements.statement: The system MUST route a complete certified-copy application to the officer designated for the level of court in which it is made.
requirements.why: Rule 383 names a different officer for each court: the Registrar or Clerk of the Court in the Sessions Court, the Clerk of the Court before a Judicial Magistrate, the Sheristedar before a Metropolitan Magistrate, and a specially authorised junior clerk where no senior clerk is appointed. An application for a free copy goes instead to the presiding officer for orders. A queue that sends everything to one role either overloads it or puts the decision with someone the rule does not empower.

binds.target: certified copy application - officer competent to grant or refuse

requirements.how: An application for a copy free of costs is placed before the presiding officer for orders; all others go to the officer designated for that court.
requirements.test: The application queue for a case in a Judicial Magistrate's court is addressed to the Clerk of the Court, and an application for a free copy is addressed to the presiding officer.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 383 names a different officer for each court: the Registrar or Clerk of the Court in the Sessions Court, the Clerk of the Court before a Judicial Magistrate, the Sheristedar in the Court of the Metropolitan Magistrate, and a junior clerk specially authorised by the Judicial Magistrate where no senior clerk is appointed; it also sends an application for a copy free of costs to the presiding officer for orders. The routing is a list in the rule rather than an inference from it.

requirements.statement: The system MUST communicate a refusal of a certified-copy application, and the grounds of the refusal, to the applicant in writing.
requirements.why: Rule 383 requires both the refusal and its grounds to be communicated in writing. A refusal shown only as a status change leaves the applicant with nothing to correct and nothing to challenge, and in a cheque case where the copy is needed for an appeal the time lost is time out of the appeal period.

binds.target: certified copy application - written refusal with grounds

requirements.test: The refuse action is unavailable until a grounds text is entered; the applicant's record then shows a written refusal document carrying that text, with the date it was despatched and the channel it went by.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 383 says that in case of refusal, such refusal and the grounds for the refusal shall be communicated to the applicant in writing. Both the communication and the grounds are directed, and it is the writing that the requirement holds.

requirements.statement: The system MUST transmit the record and proceedings of a SARAS case to the appellate or revisional court in electronic form on that court's direction.
requirements.why: Rule 14.1 makes electronic transmission the ordinary route. Where the trial record exists only on the portal, a system that can only produce a paper paging of the record either sends up a reconstruction or holds the appeal until one is made, and the appellant in a cheque case waits on an administrative task rather than a judicial one.

binds.target: record transmission on appeal or revision
