requirements.test: A direction from an appellate or revisional court produces an electronic transmission of the complete record and proceedings, with the transmission logged on the case.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 14.1 says that upon receipt of a direction from the Appellate Court or the Revisional Court, the record and proceedings of the matter as available on the designated portal shall be transmitted in electronic form to the concerned Appellate Court. The trigger, the form and the destination are all in the sub-rule.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT transmit the original record or hard copies of the electronically maintained case record except as the appellate or revisional court directs.
requirements.why: Rule 14.2 keeps the originals where they are unless the higher court asks for them. Sending up the original cheque with the appeal record removes from the trial court the very instrument SARAS rule 3.11 requires to be retained until the dispute attains finality, and it can be lost in transit between two courts neither of which is now responsible for it.

binds.target: record transmission - originals and hard copies

requirements.test: Transmission of originals or hard copies requires a recorded direction of the appellate or revisional court; the default transmission carries only the electronic record.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 14.2 says the original record and hard copies of the electronically maintained case record shall be transmitted only in accordance with, and subject to, the directions issued by the Appellate Court or the Revisional Court. The word only is the prohibition; rule 3.11, which requires the original cheque to be retained until the dispute attains finality, is what makes the restriction matter in a cheque case.

requirements.statement: The system MUST give a criminal matter presented in the High Court a filing number on presentation, and a registration number only when there is no office objection.
requirements.why: Rule 333 makes them two distinct numbers with different meanings. A system with a single number cannot express a quashing petition against a cheque complaint that has been presented but not registered, and the petitioner cannot tell whether his matter is before the court or still with the office.

binds.target: High Court criminal matter - filing number and registration number

requirements.test: A presented matter shows a filing number and no registration number; clearing the last office objection assigns the registration number and both remain on the record.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 333, as inserted in 2016, says a filing number shall initially be given to all criminal main matters, and that if there is no office objection, a registration number shall be given to the matter. Two numbers under two different conditions are what the rule creates.

requirements.statement: The system MUST complete the office examination of a criminal appeal or application in the High Court within six days of filing.
requirements.why: Rule 339 fixes six days, shortened to the next day where the sentence is six months or less and the accused is in custody. A revision against a cheque conviction that sits unscrutinised past that period delays the point at which the accused can even ask for suspension of sentence, and the shortened track exists precisely for the case where he is in custody.

binds.target: High Court scrutiny - six day examination clock

requirements.how: The examination is completed within six days of filing, except where the sentence is six months or less and the accused is in custody, in which case not later than the day after presentation or receipt.
requirements.test: A filed criminal application carries a scrutiny due date six days out, and one with a custody flag and a sentence of six months or less carries a next-day due date.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 339 says every appeal or application shall be examined by the office as expeditiously as possible and the examination completed within six days from the date of filing, except in matters in which the sentence is six months or less and the accused is in custody, where it must be completed not later than the day next after presentation or receipt. Both clocks and the condition that switches between them are in the rule.

requirements.statement: The system MUST place a criminal appeal or application before the Court for orders where the office objections are not removed within fourteen days of their notification.
requirements.why: Rule 340 gives the advocate or applicant fourteen days and then requires the matter to go before the Court without delay. Without that trigger, a quashing petition in a cheque case can sit in the objection state indefinitely while the trial below proceeds, which is exactly the outcome the petitioner filed to prevent.

binds.target: High Court objections - fourteen day removal clock

requirements.how: The office notifies objections on a special notice board and an entry of the date of notification is made on the presentation form; the fourteen days run from that notification.
requirements.test: Notification of objections starts a fourteen-day clock recorded on the matter, and on expiry without removal the matter appears on a list for orders.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 340 requires the office to affix the objections on a special notice board and to enter the date of that notification on the presentation form, and its clause (ii) says the advocate, appellant or applicant shall remove the objections within fourteen days from the date of notification, failing which the matter shall without delay be placed before the Court for orders. The period, the event it runs from and the consequence are all stated.

requirements.statement: The system MUST require a criminal appeal or application in the High Court to be accompanied by a certified copy of the judgment or order challenged.
requirements.why: Rule 345 requires every criminal appeal and application to be accompanied by the certified copy of the judgment or order challenged, and additionally by the certified copy of the trial court judgment where the challenge is to an appellate or revisional order of the Sessions Judge. A revision against a cheque conviction filed without the trial judgment is objected to at scrutiny, and the fourteen-day objection clock consumes the time the applicant needed for the certified copy in the first place. The rule says what must accompany the memorandum and leaves the manner of production open, so how is null.

binds.target: High Court filing - accompanying certified copies

requirements.test: A criminal application cannot be presented without a certified copy of the order challenged, and a challenge to a revisional order additionally requires the trial court judgment.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 345 says every appeal and application shall be accompanied by the certified copy of the judgment or order appealed from or applied against, including the certified copy of the judgment of the trial Court where the application is against an appellate or revisional order of the Sessions Judge. Both limbs are in the rule. It says what must accompany the memorandum and leaves the manner of production open, which is why how is null.

requirements.statement: The system MUST list an application to quash a complaint and a criminal revision before a Single Judge.
requirements.why: Rule 2 assigns to a Single Judge applications under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, now section 528 of the Sanhita, revisional jurisdiction under section 401, and applications to transfer or stay proceedings pending in a criminal court. Most cheque litigation that reaches the High Court arrives by one of those routes; listing it before a Division Bench wastes a board and returns the matter for relisting.

binds.target: High Court listing - Single Judge jurisdiction

requirements.test: A quashing petition and a criminal revision arising out of a cheque case are listed before a Single Judge by default, and a Division Bench listing requires an express override.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 2, in its Part II on criminal matters, assigns to a Single Judge applications for the exercise of the Court's revisional jurisdiction under section 401 of the Code, applications under section 482 of the Code, applications for transfer of cases and proceedings pending in a criminal court, and by clause (11-A) applications under article 227 of the Constitution. The routes by which cheque litigation reaches the High Court are named items in that list.

requirements.statement: The system MUST charge the fixed fee prescribed for an application to the High Court for the exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution.
requirements.why: Schedule II Article 1(f)(ii) puts fifty rupees on an Article 227 application, against one hundred rupees for an Article 226 petition not concerning fundamental rights and twenty rupees in any other case. The supervisory route under Article 227 is how an accused in a cheque case seeks to have the complaint quashed or the proceedings stayed, so the wrong entry is applied at scale.

binds.target: court fee calculation - High Court application under Article 227

requirements.how: Schedule II Article 1(f)(ii): fifty rupees on an application to the High Court for the exercise of its jurisdiction under article 227, as against one hundred rupees under Article 1(f)(i) on an article 226 petition for any purpose other than the enforcement of fundamental rights and twenty rupees under Article 1(f)(iii) in any other case.
requirements.test: An Article 227 application is charged the Article 1(f)(ii) amount, distinct from the Article 226 and residual entries.
requirements.statusReason: Schedule II Article 1(f)(ii) charges fifty rupees on an application to the High Court for directions, orders or writs under article 226 for the enforcement of a fundamental right or for the exercise of its jurisdiction under article 227, against one hundred rupees under Article 1(f)(i) for an article 226 petition for any other purpose and twenty rupees under Article 1(f)(iii) in any other case. The three rates and what separates them are the entry's own.

requirements.statement: The system MUST accept a receipt of payment made through the e-payment system in place of a stamp when the sufficiency of court fees on an appeal is inquired into.
requirements.why: Section 37(1) makes e-payment a lawful mode of collecting court fees, and rule 64 was amended to contemplate the e-payment receipt being produced where a stamp of a different amount would otherwise be required. Accepting it is therefore not a matter of the office's choice. Where the office can only accept a physical stamp, the electronic payment made at the trial court, which is how the fee is paid in an e-filed cheque case, cannot be carried into the appeal record, and the appeal is objected to for a fee that was in fact paid.

binds.target: High Court scrutiny - proof of court fee paid electronically

requirements.test: An e-payment receipt reference satisfies the court-fee sufficiency check on an appeal without a physical stamp.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 64 as amended contemplates the case where a stamp of a different amount is required on the appeal, or a receipt of payment made through the e-payment system is required to be produced, so the receipt is named in the rule as something the office calls for on the sufficiency inquiry. Section 37(1) makes e-payment a lawful mode of collecting the fee in the first place. Accepting the receipt is therefore what the amended rule provides for and not a concession the office may choose to make.

requirements.statement: The system MUST show, on the memorandum of a criminal proceeding in the High Court challenging an order of a Sessions Court whose jurisdiction covers more than one revenue district, the revenue district in which the original proceeding was instituted.
requirements.why: Rule 345 requires it, and it is what the High Court office uses to place a matter arising out of a multi-district Sessions Court. A revision against a Sessions appellate order in a cheque case that does not name the revenue district of institution is objected to at scrutiny, and the fourteen-day objection clock runs while the memorandum is corrected.

binds.target: High Court memorandum - revenue district in which the original proceeding was instituted

requirements.test: A memorandum challenging an order of a Sessions Court held in the record as covering more than one revenue district cannot be presented without the revenue district of institution recorded, and that district appears on the generated memorandum.
requirements.statusReason: The last sentence of rule 345 says that when the order complained of is that of a Sessions Court having jurisdiction over more than one revenue district, the memorandum of the proceeding shall show the revenue district in which the original proceeding was instituted. The condition and what must appear on the memorandum are both in the rule.
